title: Allye introduces 400 kW fast charger with second-life batteries - electrive.com
content:
British company Allye Energy has unveiled the MEV, a battery-buffered fast charger for depots. The system uses complete second-life batteries from EVs and is designed to provide up to 400 kW of charging power without necessarily requiring a more powerful grid connection.
The first deliveries of the MEV are planned for the second quarter of 2027.
Image: Alllye
The Mobile Energy Vault (MEV) is designed to draw energy from an existing depot power connection and initially store it in repurposed vehicle batteries. During charging, this energy can then be delivered at significantly higher power levels. According to media reports, Allye primarily targets fleet locations where the available grid connection capacity is insufficient for conventional fast charging.
At launch, two variants are planned. The MEV200 offers 155 kWh of storage capacity, while the MEV300 provides 232 kWh. Both systems are capable of charging two vehicles simultaneously. Allye specifies a maximum DC charging power of up to 400 kW.
The technical foundation is the 800-volt architecture of the Max300 mobile battery storage system. According to the manufacturer, it supports both 400-volt and 800-volt vehicle systems. The so-called PackFlex technology enables the operation of battery packs of varying sizes, ages and cell chemistries within a single system.
Allye states that it uses complete battery packs from decommissioned electric vehicles, rather than newly produced cells. Per unit, this approach is estimated to save approximately 15 to 24 tonnes of CO₂ equivalents compared to a system using new batteries. This figure is based on the manufacturer’s calculations.
Battery storage buffers weak grid connections
The approach involves decoupling grid power and charging power. The battery system can be charged over an extended period at relatively low power from the grid and then deliver this energy to vehicles at high power for short durations.
A practical example of this approach is a project by the company at
J&M Murdoch
in Glasgow. According to Allye, a grid upgrade for a waste management company’s operational depot was quoted at approximately £300,000. Instead, Allye and charging provider Chargepoly installed a Max300 unit on an existing 32 A connection with 22 kW capacity. The storage system now powers a separate DC fast charger for two electric vehicles, providing around 200 kWh of energy per day, as stated by the company.
At J&M Murdoch, a Max300 supplies two electric vehicles with around 200 kWh per day via a 22 kW connection.
This example also highlights the limitations of the concept. While a battery storage system can enable high charging power despite a weak grid connection, it does not replace the required energy volume. The number of vehicles that can be serviced daily still depends on how much electricity can be recharged via the existing connection over several hours.
Allye argues that this solution helps avoid long waiting times for new grid connections. The company points to lead times of 18 to 36 months for new depot connections in the UK. In contrast, the MEV can be installed via industrial sockets or a fixed connection and commissioned within a few hours. The system can also be dismantled and redeployed at another depot in the event of a location change.
For operation, Allye incorporates additional safety features. The charging cables are equipped with cut monitoring, forensic markings and quick-release mechanisms to facilitate faster replacement of damaged cables. Cameras monitor charging stations and cables. Inside the storage system, features such as pyrotechnic fuses, gas detection and fire barriers between battery packs are included.
The MEV remains a stationary system at the depot. In contrast, the technically related Max300 is designed for mobility and can be used, for example, as a replacement for diesel generators or to power additional charging points. Pricing for the MEV starts at £70,000. Alternatively, Allye offers the system as “EV Charging as a Service” from £1,900 per month for the MEV200. The first deliveries are scheduled for the second quarter of 2027.
With its battery storage solution, Allye addresses a well-known challenge in fleet electrification. Often, the issue is not a fundamental lack of energy at a site but rather a limitation in the immediately available grid connection capacity. Whether a battery-buffered fast charger is economically viable compared to a grid upgrade depends heavily on the location, charging profile, existing connection and the costs of potential grid reinforcement.

title: Group14 to build battery material factory in Sagunt - electrive.com
content:
US battery material manufacturer Group14, which specializes in silicon anodes, will in future also produce in Europe. The commitment to establish a production site in Spain is directly linked to a new capital increase - specifically, with a European investor.
Group14 production is already underway in South Korea.
Image: Group14
Group14 is a battery material developer specialising in silicon-carbon anodes, based in Woodinville, Washington, USA. One of the US startup’s most important investors and cooperation partners is
. Following a previous funding round in the summer of 2025, during which Porsche also made an additional investment, the company has now announced the completion of another capital increase. Specifically, this involves €150 million from an unnamed investor.
What makes this particularly interesting is that, in return for this capital increase, Group14 has committed to expanding its so-called ‘SCC55’ production to Europe. The location decision has already been made: the company has selected Sagunt in Spain as the site “for its next industrial-scale manufacturing module with an initial 10 GWh capacity,” Group14 announced. By establishing a production site in Spain, the company aims to position its battery materials “directly adjacent to key European OEM supply chains.”
In the context of Sagunt, PowerCo immediately comes to mind. The Volkswagen subsidiary is known to be building one of its major battery cell factories in this city. In the future, the plant is set to become a joint venture project
involving Gotion High-tech
. Given its close connection to Porsche, Group14 could naturally play a role in Volkswagen’s future battery ecosystem. The unnamed investor mentioned could therefore be from the Volkswagen Group or its environment. This conclusion seems plausible but remains unconfirmed.
Regardless, Group14’s SCC55 material has, according to the developers, already “commercial traction in applications such as smartphones, drones, hypercars, and eVTOL”. In the future, it is also set to be used in EV batteries. The main feature of the new material is that it enables the use of silicon-carbon anodes instead of the usual graphite in lithium-ion batteries.
This battery ingredient is therefore set to be produced at a rate of 10 GWh per year in Spain. This would increase the short-term total production capacity to 40 GWh, according to an accompanying statement. In addition to a commercial pilot plant in Woodinville that has been operational since 2021, Group14 operates another site in Sangju, Korea (with 10 GWh) and plans to open two 10-GWh facilities in Moses Lake, Washington, USA, in 2027. For the next decade, the company aims to build production capacities to the order of “hundreds of gigawatt-hours,” according to its own statements.
Rick Luebbe, CEO and co-founder of Group14 Technologies, summarises: “To truly transform the energy economy, battery material producers must be located where the batteries are made. Our expansion into Spain reflects our vision: staying nimble, building near key customer hubs, and maintaining secure, localised supply chains.”
With the new funding commitment of €150 million (approximately $169 million), the total volume of Group14’s Series D funding round has now exceeded $665 million, according to the company. As previously reported, the startup already raised $463 million from various investors in 2025. The Series D round thus spanned nearly a year and a half.
Regarding Group14’s close ties to Germany, here is a brief digression: In 2022, Porsche first
invested in the startup
as part of the Series C funding round, contributing $100 million to the then $400 million capital injection. At the time, Porsche also announced that Group14 would supply battery materials to its battery subsidiary
Cellforce
(DE). However, Porsche announced earlier this year that it would
completely shut down Cellforce
Meanwhile: in 2023, Group14 acquired the
German company Schmid Silicon
, which operates a monosilane gas production facility in the Schwarze Pumpe industrial park on the border between Saxony and Brandenburg. Monosilane gas is an important precursor for Group14’s silicon battery technology.
In 2025, V4Smart – Porsche’s renamed and acquired Varta battery subsidiary –
unveiled its second-generation battery cell
and announced that it would use Group14’s new anode material in this cell. Shortly before, German battery cell manufacturer CustomCells had also
signed a supply agreement with Group14
, though the company went insolvent just a few months later.
Another important partnership for Group14 in Germany is with the chemical company BASF. Earlier this year, both companies
unveiled a market-ready silicon anode solution
designed to replace graphite in lithium-ion batteries. This involves combining BASF’s binder Licity 2698 X F with Group14’s advanced silicon anode material, SCC55.

title: Why Solid-State Batteries Matter for Space
content:
Battery Applications
Materials
Design & Manufacturing
Thermal Management
Industry Trends
Updates on why solid-state batteries matter for space, from NASA’s lunar testing to Basquevolt and Battera’s aerospace battery advances.
October 29, 2026
3 Min Read
Yi Lin, left, SPEARS testing and research lead, and Ji Su, a polymer materials scientist and the task lead, during the removal of SPEARS batteries from thermal vacuum testing at NASA Langley.
NASA/Ryan Hill
Solid-state batteries are attracting growing interest for space and aerospace applications. Unlike conventional
lithium-ion batteries
, which use liquid electrolytes, solid-state battery designs replace that liquid with a solid material. This change can reduce limitations associated with leakage, flammability, and temperature sensitivity.
Batteries used on the Moon and in spacecraft need to withstand extreme cold, intense heat, vacuum exposure, and repeated extreme thermal cycling. In these conditions, the battery must survive harsh conditions, return to operation when needed, and do so without adding excessive weight or complexity to the vehicle or system.
Two recent announcements illustrate how solid-state battery development is progressing from different directions. Developments from NASA and a collaboration between Basquevolt and Battera Technologies suggest that solid-state batteries are moving closer to practical use in space-related systems.
Related:
Robot Dogs & Mobile Chargers Power Up Detroit's Smart Parking Test Bed
NASA’s SPEARS project and the challenge of lunar conditions
NASA’s announcement centers on its Solid Power for Extreme Environment Adaptability and Resilience in Space (SPEARS) project. The goal is to develop batteries that can help support sustained human and robotic activity on the Moon, especially near the lunar South Pole, where temperatures can drop from 212°F to about -328°F.
Traditional lithium-ion batteries are poorly suited to this environment because their liquid electrolytes can freeze in severe cold, become unstable at high temperatures, or evaporate in vacuum. NASA’s solid-state approach aims to address these issues by using ceramic- or polymer-based solid electrolytes.
According to the agency, recent thermal vacuum tests at NASA Langley Research Center showed that small prototype cells operated well up to 176°F and down to -76°F, with somewhat reduced performance at -112°F. “We proved for the first time that these cells can work down to minus -112°F,” stated Yi Lin, SPEARS testing and research lead at NASA Langley. Lin also stated he’s confident they can improve performance and maybe even expand that range in coming years.
Nike Lin, a support engineer/technician on the thermal vacuum team, takes weight measurements of batteries following thermal vacuum testing. Courtesy of NASA/Ryan Hill.
NASA noted that while the batteries would not function at the lowest temperatures without warming, small heaters could bring them back to operating condition. This could reduce the need for larger thermal management systems, lowering system mass and potentially extending mission duration.
NASA sees possible uses for these batteries in astronaut emergency kits, drills and tools used in shadowed craters, rovers, and scientific instruments designed for long-duration missions. “The potential market for solid-state batteries is very broad,” stated Ji Su, a polymer materials scientist and the task lead at NASA Langley. “Automobiles, cell phones, communication devices, drones — anything that needs a portable power supply.”
Related:
Public-Private Collaboration Advances Nuclear Power for Space Exploration
Basquevolt and Battera technologies target aerospace deployment
The announcement from Basquevolt and Battera Technologies highlights a more commercially oriented pathway for solid-state batteries in aerospace. These two companies said they will work together to develop next-generation integrated battery solutions for high-performance aerospace applications. The collaboration combines Basquevolt’s lithium-metal solid-state cell technology with Battera’s expertise in battery system development, manufacturing, and industrialization.
A key feature of the announcement is the emphasis on energy density. Basquevolt states that its current cells already exceed 400 watt-hours per kilogram, and the partnership is targeting more than 500 watt-hours per kilogram in the coming months. For aerospace applications, where weight has a direct effect on performance, this is a significant benchmark. They have also set a target of series production in 2027, indicating that the project is intended to move beyond research and into industrial-scale deployment.
Related:
Which Battery Company Will Supply Which Carmaker in 2026?
Basquevolt solid-state battery. Courtesy of Basquetvolt.
"This collaboration marks a pivotal step in Basquevolt's strategy to deploy our technology in the highest-value applications where energy density is not a convenience but a critical requirement," stated Pablo Fernández Santos, Managing Director of Basquevolt.
Taken together, these two developments show that solid-state batteries are being pursued both as mission-enabling technologies for space exploration and as advanced commercial products for aerospace use. Important challenges remain, including validation, integration, and large-scale manufacturing.

title: RELEX Solutions: Can Retailers Connect End-to-End Planning?

RELEX Solutions: Can Retailers Connect End-to-End Planning?
Prioritise Us
on Google
RELEX is helping organisations with inventory management and consumer demand. Credit: Getty Images
As supply chains are becoming increasingly complex, automation and forecasting are crucial for supporting resilient and intelligent decision-making
There are more opportunities and solutions for supply chains now than ever before, but this creates an issue of its own when decision makers cannot choose the most optimal solution.
RELEX Solutions is an AI platform, helping drive intelligent decision-making and
automation across complex operations
Around the world, more than 600 customers across retail, manufacturing and wholesale trust RELEX to offer support on demand, inventory and supply chain operations.
Navigating demand
In recent years, supply chains have been facing growing pressure. Demand is increasing, with both internal and external pressures building tensions for teams.
Leaders are having to manage more precise legislation, act more sustainably, integrate promotions, meet fluctuating consumer demand and cut costs. This is pulling them in different directions – for example, a strong sustainability plan might demonstrate long-term benefits, but the immediate cost may be unjustifiable as a short-term expense.
With complexity growing, businesses are
turning more towards AI
and technology to help them make decisions and meet productivity demands. RELEX Solutions offers leaders an insightful perspective, using connected forecasting, replenishment, pricing and production-planning capabilities.
At a glance
RELEX was founded in 2005
More than 2,300 employees make up the company
6,000+ customers around the world trust RELEX
Food retailers are seeing 40% reduction in food waste due to RELEX
RELEX was founded to help companies grow to scale | RELEX Co-Founders Johanna Småros, Mikko Kärkkäinen and Michael Falck. Credit: RELEX
AI in supply chain
RELEX provides a unified, AI-native platform for retailers, manufactures and wholesalers to improve forecast accuracy, optimise inventory, pricing, merchandising and production. It helps leaders to plan seamlessly across end-to-end solutions, from product production to shop-floor shelf.
Its platform combines built-in AI and agentic AI with retail and supply chain knowledge. Through this, customers are seeing higher product availability, increased sales, smarter decisions and scaled profitable growth.
The company has solutions across the entire supply chain, from demand planning and inventory & replenishment to store operations and pricing. These solutions can be applied across a variety of industries, including clothing, technology and food items.
RELEX was founded on the core principles of ‘retail’ and ‘excellence’, with a goal of making the
consumer goods value chain
more efficient and adaptable.
“It was our dream to build a successful and virtuous software company that follows our core values,” explains Mikko Kärkkäinen, Co-Founder and CEO of RELEX.
AI has been used by RELEX for years, working to increase forecast demand capabilities, optimise inventory and power supply chains that are adaptable. It also understands that the tools themselves need to be right for the businesses in order to make the best change – therefore it can be adapted for each solution.
Mikko Kärkkäinen, CEO and Co-founder at RELEX Solutions
Driving company growth
As one of Mexico’s leading retailers and distributors of wine and spirits, Grupo Vinoteca needed a means of keeping up with its wide product base and its consumer demand. It
managed demand planning
, allocation and replenishment separately, meaning it struggled to keep pace with new clients and manage seasonal shifts.
In 2023, it implemented RELEX forecasting and replenishment and integrated supply chain planning across its network. Now, Grupo Vinoteca has accurate demand forecasts across each product, store and channel.
It can track demand for each vintage, with optimised inventory planning at all times. Through this partnership, lost retail sales fell by 34.7%, reflecting improved product availability across stores and online channels. Now, the company is able to deliver ongoing annual savings, increased operations and company growth.
Key companies
CEO: Mikko Kärkkäinen
HQ: Finland
Relex Solutions is a leading supply chain and retail planning platform provider, offering AI-powered solutions for demand forecasting, inventory optimization, and workforce management. Serving major retailers and consumer goods companies globally, Relex helps businesses reduce waste, improve efficiency, and enhance customer satisfaction through advanced automation and machine learning. The company has experienced rapid growth across Europe, North America, and Asia-Pacific markets.
M&S Food

Marks & Spencer Food is the grocery division of British retail icon M&S, renowned for premium-quality prepared meals, fresh produce, and innovative food products. With over 1,000 stores including standalone M&S Foodhalls, the brand emphasizes quality, sustainability, and British sourcing. M&S Food has successfully positioned itself as a destination for special occasions and convenient, high-quality everyday meals, maintaining strong customer loyalty.
PetSmart

HQ: Arizona, US
PetSmart is North America's largest specialty pet retailer, operating over 1,600 stores offering pet supplies, grooming, training, boarding, and veterinary services through partnerships. The company provides comprehensive pet care solutions including its Banfield Pet Hospital locations and dog training facilities. PetSmart emphasizes pet adoption partnerships, sustainability initiatives, and omnichannel retail experiences, competing alongside its e-commerce subsidiary Chewy.
CEO: Raymond Cloosterman
HQ: Netherlands
Rituals Cosmetics is a luxury home and body cosmetics brand inspired by Eastern wellness traditions. Founded in 2000, the company combines ancient Asian philosophies with modern luxury, offering products spanning skincare, home fragrances, and bath items. With over 1,000 stores across 36 countries, Rituals emphasizes mindfulness, self-care rituals, and sustainable practices, creating immersive retail experiences that transform daily routines into meaningful moments.
The Body Shop
CEO: Mike Jatania
HQ: England
The Body Shop, pioneer of ethical beauty retail, faces restructuring after entering administration in 2024. Founded by Anita Roddick in 1976, the brand championed cruelty-free cosmetics, natural ingredients, and social activism. Despite its influential legacy in sustainable beauty and fair trade practices, the company struggled with financial challenges under various ownerships, leading to store closures and operational restructuring across multiple markets.
The Home Depot

The Home Depot is the world's largest home improvement retailer, operating over 2,300 stores across North America. Offering building materials, tools, appliances, and services for DIY customers and professional contractors, the company leads through extensive product selection, competitive pricing, and installation services. The Home Depot invests heavily in digital transformation, supply chain innovation, and professional customer segments while maintaining strong financial performance.

title: Exploring the Role of Flexibility in Supply Chain Management
content:
Exploring the Role of Flexibility in Supply Chain Management
Prioritise Us
on Google
Supply Chain Digital speaks to Dennis Schmitz from Arvato about helping clients manage demand. Credit: Arvato
Dennis Schmitz, Managing Director of Arvato UK, discusses how technology and forecasting help retailers prepare for peak demand and navigate complexity
Dennis Schmitz has worked at Arvato for more than 13 years, working in various roles and undertaking management roles across Europe, Asia and the US.
In 2025, Dennis became the Managing Director of UK operations at the company, which has grown significantly as a branch in the last few years.
In his role, one of Dennis’ core priorities is to set the company up for continuous growth. Within ArvatoHub, the company is organised by various industries, with dedicated solutions for each.
global 3PL service provider
, the company specialises in supply chain management and ecommerce, working to drive precise and reliable supply chain strategies to its customers. The company serves five industries, including tech, healthcare, fashion, beauty and marketplaces.
Supply Chain Digital sat down with Dennis to hear about some of the challenges Arvato has faced and the solutions it is implementing into its operations.
What are some of the biggest challenges that Arvato has seen in recent years?
We've seen challenges for our more consumer oriented brands, and I think there are three dominant key challenges.
One is disruption or supply chain resilience. There's lots of distress due to geopolitical challenges that have an impact on supply chain availability of products and delays.
Second, for our fashion clients – cost pressure. Margins are tight and there's fierce competition, particularly in the lower to mid budget, and as we see a more negative outlook on consumerism in Europe. We have been trying to navigate that with or on behalf of our clients.
Thirdly, flexibility, which is somewhat linked to resilience. Nowadays, as a retailer, you need to respond to changes in consumer behaviour so swiftly, you never know which product will take off, what demand you can generate. There’s also some complexity in channels as well. Maybe one product is particularly popular in retail, but doesn't work in ecommerce or the other way around. Acknowledging that – not only from an inventory perspective, but also from a marketing perspective – is a key challenge and requires us to have adopted our processes and the way we do logistics quite significantly.
What processes have you adopted in order to help retailers prepare for peak demand?
Forecasting. You will always hear that as part of those conversations. On the one hand, we're working closely with our clients to improve their data, but, with many of those, we have been working for quite a few years. So we've also built our own database where we can do our own analysis and data crunching.
What we have seen as a trend in the past year is that many of our clients consolidate logistics across channels within one warehouse. So there's quite a few businesses where we do operate ecommerce, retail and wholesale out of one facility. In the past, it was more usual to have a provider, one warehouse for ecommerce, another one for retail and wholesale.
This gives the opportunity to be more specific and tailor your services to the needs of a particular channel, but it poses the challenge that you need to orchestrate your inventories way more effectively. If you bring it all together, you have one inventory and you can see what works best in which channel.
When we look at automation, we explore how we can use that to the benefit of as many processes as possible. We have one fashion client at our facility, where we do operate both the ecommerce as well as the retail business. We have an auto store up and running, which normally you would mostly use for ecommerce orders, but we also use it for the retail business.
You have the benefit of the flexibility of automation to push volumes out, benefitting both the ecommerce channel and the retail one. I think that's the type of flexibility that clients look for. There's then always an additional step with additional tagging, but the baseline is already established by leveraging the technology that is out there. The combination of inventory efficiency alongside leveraging automation is our means to address some of the increased demands and flexibility from the client side.
Arvato at a glance
Arvato has more than 100 sites across Europe, the Middle East, Asia-Pacific and the Americas
It has more than 3 million metres-squared of warehouse space
Its warehouses use 100% green energy
Arvato serves 220 countries
The company has a carrier-agnostic network of 150+ carriers
Why is flexibility so crucial, particularly in today's market and how can it be integrated efficiently?
Consumer behaviour changes constantly. You never really know which collection will take off. As a retailer, you need to be in a position to react swiftly.
Our way to tackle it is through automation, both from an infrastructure perspective and from a technical perspective, like auto screening,
wave planning in the warehouse
, forecasting and orchestration of workload.
As we entertain quite a few multi-user warehouses, we have the flexibility of balancing workforce across different accounts because, while there might be a high demand and people for one client, it might be a more quiet time for another. You're in a position to balance your labour accordingly. It's all around eliminating friction in processes as much as you can.
As a 3PL, you're limited in what you can do, so you need to work together with your clients. One of our clients has introduced RFID techs for all of their products, which is quite a significant shift. It requires that client to talk to their manufacturers and to have an RFID tech with every single piece of apparel. That's ideal from a 3PL perspective, because of automatic counting, which reduces workloads and is cost effective. It's also much more frictionless.
This is where technology can be very powerful, not only in terms of cost effectiveness, but also just
getting rid of friction
in the overall supply chain.
We also find, what is key for our clients is the opportunity to grow and to scale. We're serving a lot of clients that are growing in the marketplace, and all of them want to have the benefit of 3PL to have a cost-effective setup, but still not wanting to be limited when it comes to the growth objectives. If you have a growing retailer with growing brands, they want to work with somebody who is able to scale efficiently.
Dennis explores how flexibility is crucial. Credit: Arvato
As supply chains are becoming more automated, how do you think the role of technology is going to change?
We will see a massive change in both automation robotics as well as the technology that is being used. I think the key use 3PL going forward will be orchestrating all of it and making sense of the tools that are available. Everybody can put a robot next to a conveyor belt, but having it work effectively, manage issues, plan maintenance and decide what kind of robot makes sense, is still where a lot of intelligence and brain needs to be put into the thought process.
Transitioning to a higher degree of automation would be the natural progression. This will lead to a shift in the kind of jobs you will see in a warehouse, from more standard activities to more elevated jobs and activities going forwards.
There shouldn't be technologies just for the sake of technology. It should always be tailored to the needs and the requirements of a particular business. Sometimes it's still more cost effective to do a manual process because the volume isn't there.
We always ask ourselves how technology can help and alleviate some of the pressure that we have because of scarcity of labour and other challenges. It's about being technology agnostic and finding something that fits the purposes and the requirements of the business, but is also flexible enough to be able to adapt over the course of time.
Arvato implements technology and automation in its warehouses where it sees potential. Credit: Arvato
If you were to say there was one key to supply chain resilience, what would it be?
You need to have a proper game plan in place as a client alongside your 3PL that you're working with. It's not realistic to be prepared for every eventuality, but you have a clear picture around certain scenarios. It’s important to have that contingency being defined and have a pragmatic approach on how to deal with it. It puts you in a position of being able to control it, which is where technology and data can help.
You need transparency on things that could go wrong, do a bit of
scenario planning and then define pragmatic measures
of how you would deal with it, otherwise, you always have the threat of going to extremes.
For some large scale and critical supply chains, that's what you need to be doing. And particularly for our healthcare businesses, we have setups where if we have an issue in a warehouse in Germany, the warehouse in France could step in and you have an operation that is almost flawless, but in other areas that's just not cost effective and reasonable.
You need to do a bit of scenario planning to be aware of what would be the contingency that you need to pull. I think, in the end, it comes down to having transparency and the data available to yourself.

title: Hitachi Digital, Physical AI and Manufacturing
content:
Hitachi Digital, Physical AI and Manufacturing
Prioritise Us
on Google
Hitachi Digital will combine GlobalLogic and Hitachi Digital Services under one brand from April 2027,
Hitachi Digital CEO Anand Birje outlines cloud, data and physical AI for supply chain and other complex industries
Hitachi is launching Hitachi Digital, a global digital services company designed to help manufacturing and other asset-intensive industries connect cloud, data and artificial intelligence with measurable operational outcomes.
Scheduled to begin legal operations on 1 April 2027, Hitachi Digital will combine GlobalLogic and Hitachi Digital Services under one brand. The new company will bring together software engineering, enterprise systems, operational technology (OT), cloud, data and AI capabilities for complex industries including energy, mobility and manufacturing and their respective supply chains.
Hitachi Digital targets industrial transformation
Hitachi Digital will have approximately 35,000 professionals, operations in 27 countries and more than 880 active clients.
The business will support organisations across the digital and physical layers of operations, including: cloud transformation, data and intelligence, digital operations and and physical AI.
Other enterprise services include software and product engineering, site reliability engineering (SRE), enterprise systems integration, AI development and deployment and operational technology modernisation.
The company will be headquartered in Santa Clara, California, and led by Anand Birje, Chief Executive Officer and Chairman.
The executive’s original launch statement said Hitachi Digital would combine digital engineering and operations at global scale, supported by Hitachi’s industrial experience in mission-critical infrastructure.
Anand Birje, CEO and Chairman, Hitachi Digital
Physical AI connects data to supply chain operations
Physical AI refers to artificial intelligence operating in or interacting with the physical world. In the supply chain sphere, applications may include autonomous and semi-autonomous supply chains, robotics, autonomous vehicles and AI-supported safety systems.
Hitachi Digital will focus on physical AI alongside:
Enterprise AI
Industrial data platforms
Cloud architecture
Digital twins
Robotics
Edge intelligence
Connected products
Asset performance
Operational resilience
The company said its physical AI strategy will be supported by Hitachi’s long-standing OT and industry knowledge. Target sectors include manufacturing, mobility and energy, with supply chain positioned within the wider industrial and mission-critical market opportunity.
For supply chain operators, the value proposition is the connection between digital systems and physical operations. Rather than treating AI as a standalone software layer, Hitachi Digital aims to deploy it within environments such as manufacturing plants, fulfilment sites, depots and logistics networks.
Hitachi Digital will be focusing on physical AI among other service offerings.
Forward-Deployed Engineers work at the operational edge
A central element of Hitachi Digital’s model is its use of Forward-Deployed Engineers (FDEs).
FDE teams, including AI specialists, data scientists and engineers, work alongside customers and technology partners in operational environments. Their role is to apply digital capabilities to real business processes rather than develop systems in isolation.
In addition to industry specific workflows in manufacturing and supply chain, FDEs could support digital control rooms, operational data capture, AI governance, safety and reliability workflows and wider integration between
enterprise
and OT systems.
Hitachi said the teams will help capture operational rules, technical know-how and tacit knowledge from frontline environments. That information can then support HMAX, Hitachi’s AI suite for social infrastructure.
HMAX grounds AI in industrial context
HMAX by Hitachi is described as a next-generation suite that brings AI capabilities to social infrastructure.
The platform is intended to help translate operational knowledge into AI-enabled systems. For individual manufacturing sectors, this could be important because industrial AI must account for site conditions, equipment constraints, production targets, safety requirements and regulatory obligations.
Hitachi’s model is based on a feedback loop in which FDEs work alongside operational teams. After the engineer teams capture rules and frontline knowledge, the resultant data and context are incorporated into AI systems.
The insight generated by AI-backed tools is then used to support operational decisions and workflows. Each deployment generates further knowledge for future use. This iterative approach is designed to make AI more context-aware and reliable in complex physical environments.
Hitachi becomes customer zero
Hitachi Digital will serve external customers while also supporting Hitachi’s own transformation programme.
The company will work with Hitachi business units including Energy, Mobility and Connective Industries. FDEs are expected to operate alongside teams at locations such as depots, substations and plants.
Hitachi’s internal businesses therefore become a customer zero: a live environment in which digital and physical AI solutions can be tested, refined and scaled before being applied more broadly.
The company said synergy revenue with the Hitachi Group grew 46% year on year in the first half.
Cloud, data and AI enter a convergence zone
Hitachi Digital’s launch is based on the view that cloud, data and
are no longer separate technology programmes.
Hitachi Digital describes a convergence period between 2025 and 2027, as organisations increasingly seek one partner capable of delivering all three capabilities together.
For manufacturing companies and their supply chain divisions, Hitachi expects this convergence to support:
Cloud-based operational platforms
Real-time data from manufacturing, distribution and fulfilment sites
Integrated enterprise and OT systems
Secure AI deployment
Scalable digital products
The strategic challenge is not only implementing an AI model. It is connecting that model to the data, infrastructure, workflows and physical assets needed to create measurable value.
Penske Logistics has achieved substantial cost savings and improved operational reliability via its partnership with Hitachi Digital. (Credit: Getty)
Digital engineering and enterprise operations unite
GlobalLogic contributes digital engineering, product development and software capabilities. Hitachi Digital Services contributes enterprise systems, cloud, infrastructure and operational expertise.
Under Hitachi Digital, the combined organisation will operate as a single global company using the Hitachi brand.
Hitachi Digital will also support adoption of Lumada 3.0, Hitachi’s digital solutions and co-creation platform. Lumada is positioned as a mechanism for working with customers to develop digital solutions for industrial and social infrastructure challenges. The company said its engineering and operational expertise will continue to support intellectual property development, including HMAX and Lumada 3.0.
The new structure will include Hitachi Digital Inc. as the operating company serving clients.
Industry sectors and supply chain relevance
Hitachi Digital will target a range of vertical markets, including:
Automotive and mobility
Banking, financial services and insurance
Healthcare and life sciences
High technology and semiconductors
Industrial and manufacturing
Logistics
Energy and utilities
Media and entertainment
Retail and consumer packaged goods
Telecommunications and networking
Supply chain sits within the wider industrial, energy, mobility and logistics ecosystem. Its relevance to Hitachi Digital’s strategy comes from the sector’s need to integrate physical assets, operational technology, enterprise systems, data platforms and AI.

Its industrial footprint spans energy, mobility, digital systems and social infrastructure. Hitachi will act both as the new company’s owner and as a customer zero, using Hitachi Digital to support internal transformation across operational businesses.

Exotec: Scaling Warehouse Automation for Fulfilment Networks
Prioritise Us
on Google
Warehouses are seeing gains in efficiency, cost savings and productivity since adopting Exotec. Credit: Exotec
Exotec is creating a connected fulfilment network with scaled automation, resulting in efficiency gains, cost savings and greater worker productivity
As demand for efficient operations grows and technology becomes more innovative, warehouses are rolling out more automation across their operations.
This creates a challenge of its own – what can be automated, what needs to be automated and can this be scaled across multiple warehouses in the network?
Exotec builds warehouse robotic solutions and aims to help develop a standardised design, taking automation from a singular warehouse,
to a connected fulfilment network
Meeting complex demands
Supply chains are becoming more complex, driven by increasing volatility, growing demand, rising costs and pressures to operate more efficiently and more cost-effectively. Facing pressures such as this, supply chain leaders are turning towards automation as a solution to meet demand, streamline manual processes and cut costs.
Though robotics are a large investment, they are seen as a cost-effective solution, as the return on investment occurs in the form of efficiency, productivity and long-term cost savings. By
automating a warehouse
, the number of human staff required get cut significantly, or they get placed onto workflows that cannot be automated.
Exotec designs and installs flexible solutions that offer a fast return on investment. The solutions can adapt to demand without disrupting normal operations, and works with the client to define operational objectives. This results in connected systems that accelerate ROI and can continue to grow as the company scales.
Exotec’s warehouse execution software, Deepsky, operates as a single orchestration layer, connecting the client’s warehouse management systems to its entire automation ecosystem. This means that all hardware operates under a unified software, resulting in a simplified operation with improved performance.
It offers precise identification of the content and location of every container within the solution, providing full traceability. It also offers live KPIs, system status and performance insights with a personalised dashboard.
With real-time data, leaders get a full picture of their order release, picking flows and replenishment, resulting in greater understanding of warehouse operations. Leaders can access all inventory in two minutes or less with Deepsky.
Automation is most valuable when it supports both growth and people.
James Schlechter, Business Development Leader at Exotec
Exotec’s Skypod system has revolutionised warehouse efficiency. Credit: Exotec
Scaling warehouse automation
In March 2026, Exotec announced the deployment of a multi-site program for Decathlon, demonstrating how
warehouse automation could be scaled
across multiple sites within a network.
Skyfleet was deployed in seven warehouses across France, the UK, Portugal, Italy and Germany. This meant Decathlon could standardise supply chain flows across Europe, gain greater management across the sites and improve the working environment for its staff.
Skyfleet is an example of Exotec as both an OEM and an integrator, simplifying processes and accelerating scaled deployments.
Each Skyfleet warehouse has
A fleet of 150-200 Skypod robots
100,000 - 125,000 storage locations
Capacity for 3,000 - 4,000 lines an hour
150,000 - 200,000 items per day
7 to 13 picking stations
Parcel buffering before shipping
Full automation of inbound and outbound flows
In order to maximise warehouse intralogistics automation, additional automated
equipment is strategically integrated
into each site. This includes automatic palletisers and depalletisers, RFID tunnels and automatic carton opening machine.
Standardising the machines across these operations has resulted in significant cost and efficiency savings. Through automating manual tasks, teammates can instead grow their skills in other areas.
“Automation is most valuable when it supports both growth and people,” writes James Schlechter, Business Development Leader at Exotec on LinkedIn.
In Decathlon’s Northampton, UK site, a picker now walks only one kilometer per day, as opposed to its previous 10km. Alongside this, workplace incidents related to order picking have now decreased from one in 5,000 to one in 10,000.
Operations are now more efficient and more cost-effective, creating better workflows in order to meet higher demand, as well as creating better working conditions, thus
maintaining staff safety and productivity
James Schlechter, Business Development Leader at Exotec

title: Volkswagen hits pause on the Golf EV as it faces an 'urgent need for action'
content:
Volkswagen
Peter Johnson
| Oct 30 2026 - 7:29 am PT
Volkswagen
has put the electric Golf on hold for now as it faces growing pressure to cut costs.
Volkswagen is suspending Golf EV development for now
“We cannot afford to lose any time and must act quickly and decisively,” Volkswagen Group CFO and COO Arno Antlitz warned after the company reported its largest quarterly loss since the “Dieselgate” scandal in 2015 on Thursday.
VW Group’s operating loss swelled to €5.9 billion ($6.5 billion) in the third quarter because of a write-down of its Porsche stake, weak sales in China, and lower profit margins on electric vehicles.
As part of its latest cost-control efforts, Volkswagen is pausing development of the all-electric Golf at its Wolfsburg plant in Germany.
“We simply can’t afford this work right now,” VW brand CEO Thomas Schäfer said in an internal memo
reviewed on Friday. The Wolfsburg plant, or the “heart of the VW brand,” is about €300 million ($334.5 million) short of its cost-cutting targets, the memo said.
Volkswagen Golf EV preview (Source: Volkswagen)
Schäfer said the “decision was really not an easy one for us,” knowing what the Golf means to Wolfsburg.
The decision comes after Volkswagen’s Supervisory Board approved its restructuring strategy, “Future Plan 2030,” last month, which includes reducing its global workforce by 100,000, trimming its lineup, and closing several plants in Germany.
Volkswagen initially planned to launch the Golf EV in 2028, but Schäfer confirmed earlier this year that the electric hatch
will be delayed
until closer to 2030.
Volkswagen Golf GTI Edition 50 (Source: Volkswagen)
Schäfer suggested the delay was because the SSP (Scalable Systems Platform), developed through its partnership with Rivian, was taking longer than expected.
The electric Golf, which is expected to arrive as the ID. Golf, will be one of the first vehicles based on the new platform.
While development is on hold, VW’s works council said the pause will not delay the Golf EV’s launch, promising to make up for lost time. It’s still expected to launch in 2030.
Volkswagen will begin building the electric Golf in Wolfsburg closer to the end of the decade, while production of the gas-powered model will move to Mexico in 2027.

title: Waymo picks Toyota bZ4X as its next robotaxi, starting in Japan in 2027
content:
Robotaxi
autonomous driving
Toyota bZ4X
Fred Lambert
| Oct 30 2026 - 6:22 am PT
Waymo is adding the Toyota bZ4X to its robotaxi lineup. Toyota will build a custom version of the electric SUV with the Waymo Driver integrated right on the line in Japan, and a test fleet will start operating there in 2027.
It’s the first actual vehicle to come out of the partnership the two companies signed last year. And it gives Waymo a Japanese-built car for its Tokyo launch, with the UK and other markets to follow.
When Waymo and Toyota
first announced their deal in April 2025
, it was a preliminary agreement to “explore” working together on autonomous driving, including in personally owned vehicles. Lots of intent, no product.
Now there’s a product. According to
Waymo’s announcement
, Toyota will produce the vehicles at its Takaoka plant in Toyota City, Aichi Prefecture, and Waymo’s self-driving hardware will be installed and integrated at that same site instead of being retrofitted somewhere else.
The robotaxi bZ4X gets a few rider-focused changes: extra rear legroom, automatic doors, a power liftgate, and ambient lighting. Waymo didn’t share sensor specs, unit volumes, or what each vehicle costs.
Operations in 2027 are about testing and validating the autonomous bZ4X fleet in Japan. The UK and “other Waymo markets” come in later years, with no dates attached.
The two companies also say they’ll keep working on autonomous tech for Toyota’s personal vehicles, plus safety projects with Woven by Toyota, the automaker’s software arm.
Waymo co-CEO Dmitri Dolgov said that “Toyota’s commitment to zero traffic accidents resonates deeply with us at Waymo.”
Waymo now has four vehicle platforms
The timing lines up with Waymo’s Japan plans. In September, Waymo said it’s
targeting fully driverless commercial rides in Tokyo in 2027
with taxi operator Nihon Kotsu and ride-hailing app GO, scaling to about 100 vehicles, pending regulatory approval.
In the US, Waymo’s fleet is still mostly made up of Jaguar I-Pace SUVs, a model Jaguar no longer produces. It’s been adding the Zeekr-built Ojai van and the Hyundai Ioniq 5, and Hyundai is reportedly in talks to
supply up to 50,000 Ioniq 5 robotaxis by 2028
The bZ4X makes four. It isn’t Toyota’s first robotaxi bZ4X either: Toyota and Pony.ai started mass-producing bZ4X-based robotaxis in China earlier this year.
For US readers, the refreshed model is sold here simply as the Toyota bZ, starting at $34,900. A cheap, high-volume base vehicle matters a lot when you’re trying to scale a fleet.
And Waymo is scaling. It now does over 500,000 paid rides a week across 15 US metros, and it
picked Toronto as its first Canadian city
earlier this month, with riders targeted for 2028.
Electrek’s Take
This is a big one, even if the bZ4X is about as exciting as a toaster.
Waymo’s biggest constraint right now is cars. It has been running a fleet built on a discontinued Jaguar, and every new automaker it signs adds manufacturing capacity it doesn’t have to build itself. Toyota is the world’s best-selling automaker. Having it build Waymo-ready vehicles on its own assembly line is exactly the kind of industrial partner Waymo needed.
Yes, the bZ4X had a rough start (Toyota recalled the first batch in 2022 because the wheels could come off). But it has come a long way now – becoming boring and reliable. And for a robotaxi, boring and reliable is the whole point.
Compare that with Tesla’s approach: a two-seat Cybercab with no steering wheel, built in-house, with a self-certified autonomy stack that still isn’t operating at anything close to Waymo’s scale. Waymo keeps plugging its driver into existing EVs from established automakers and expanding city by city. So far, that’s working.
The way it is looking now. It sounds like Toyota will take over manufacturing Waymo driver cars for right-hand-drive markets. But what interests me most is the personal-vehicle angle. Toyota and Waymo keep mentioning it, but there’s still nothing concrete. If Toyota actually puts the Waymo Driver in a car you can buy, Tesla’s FSD Supervised pitch gets a lot harder to sell. Will that happen before the end of the decade? Who knows.

title: Jasion Poki review: The Electric Minibike that packs heavy-duty fun
content:
Seth Weintraub
| Oct 30 2026 - 5:42 am PT
In our transportation reporting, we rarely come across something as fun as today’s review of the
Jasion Poki.
The Poki is a severely overpowered electric minibike that looks like it came from yesteryear. If the power isn’t enough, it also packs some cool tricks, and we’re not (just) talking about wheelies this time.
Jasion Poki by the numbers:
Massive peak power from its central mid-drive motor. There’s a 2kW label on our early review model, which we reviewed thinking something was up. Turns out we were right; this is a powerhouse.
260 N·m:
Raw, low-end torque to launch the bike forward. And Wheelies!
60V 30Ah:
The hefty lithium-ion battery capacity built into the base chassis. Under the seat with a relatively high center of gravity..
Jasion’s top speed. As a 200lber, I acheived 44mph crouched on flat ground. It shouldn’t even go this fast. I don’t think it would hit 50 without a 90-pounder wearing lycra behind the handlebars.
60 miles of range
: At 30-40mph, expect closer to half that range
137.5 lbs:
The substantial net weight of the bike, making it a heavy lift for manual transport.
So taking a look at this bad boy, it just screams fun. It is really low to the ground, has a big, wide seat large enough for 2 people as long as they are under 350lbs total, and has pegs for 2 people and a basket, great for carrying a picnic and an extra helmet.
Heavy duty
This thing is built like a tank, and it tips the scales accordingly. Getting this thing in my SUV ruptured a few discs in my back, though its compact nature means it fit quite well. Loosen the handlebars and it is downright compact. But that weight is strangely like 50lbs heavier than I would expect at close to 140lbs.
That also makes the built-in wheelies a little bit more suspect. My son, who is by now becoming an expert at wheelies, found this one to be a bit more difficult than the auto wheelies on bikes like the Anyland or new Yozma IN11.
The fun part
OK so not only does this little powerhouse get you (and your friend) around town in style and it also makes wheelies a bit easier; but it also has a huge Bluetooth speaker in the back that sounds like a Harley and is all synced up with the actual controller so it sounds real.
Sure, it is a gimmick, but it is a fun one, and it might actually make the low-down bike a little safer since it is going to be out of the sight of most cars.
Electrek’s take:
I love this thing. It is my favorite bike to go to the beach on (and it does well in the sand with those fat tires). But I think there are some big misses here. First of all, it has no business going over 40mph. Not only does it feel scary with those tiny wheels, but speed wobbles puts both the rider a possible second rider at significant risk here. This is a fun bike and it should top out at 20-28mph max. Keep all the torque, just cut out the power at a reasonable top speed.
Also it should weigh a lot less. At 140lbs, it is silly hard to get into the back of a car, which it easily fits in. Making the frame aluminum would go a long way here. Also, if this thing rolled on top of you, it would be a bad day.
Make this thing safer and more portable, and I’d recommend everyone with a beach commute to get one. As it stands, best for responsible adults with strong backs and a Peter Pan complex.

title: Harley-Davidson’s electric motorcycle brand LiveWire warns it may not survive
content:
Electric Motorcycles
LiveWire
Micah Toll
| Oct 30 2026 - 1:10 am PT
Harley-Davidson-born electric motorcycle maker
LiveWire
has issued a troubling warning about its financial future, announcing that it has substantial doubt about its ability to continue operating as a going concern. The news sent LiveWire’s stock plunging more than 40% on Thursday morning as the company withdrew its full-year financial guidance.
The announcement comes despite some signs of improving sales, with LiveWire reporting a 38% increase in third-quarter revenue to $7.9 million and a 21% rise in motorcycle unit sales. However, the company continues to burn through cash, reporting a net loss of $18.6 million for the quarter.
LiveWire’s cash reserves have also dwindled significantly, falling from $82.8 million at the end of 2025 to just $39.9 million as of September 30, 2026.
The company has now formed a special restructuring committee to explore potential financing arrangements, strategic partnerships, investments, or even a sale. It also withdrew its previous guidance projecting a $70 million to $80 million operating loss for 2026.
The financial warning comes at a particularly pivotal moment for LiveWire, which is
preparing to launch its most affordable electric motorcycles yet.
The upcoming LiveWire S4 Honcho series represents a major departure from the company’s existing premium electric motorcycles, offering smaller, lighter, and significantly more affordable models designed to attract a much broader audience of riders with a starting price below US $5,000.
LiveWire S4 Honcho Street electric motorcycle
The lower prices could dramatically increase LiveWire’s sales volumes, especially as the company attempts to move beyond the relatively small market for high-dollar electric motorcycles. The Honcho lineup is also expected to help lower the barrier to entry for new riders, with approachable electric motorcycles that eliminate the complexity of clutch and gear shifting.
LiveWire is also preparing to
showcase its latest developments at EICMA in Milan next week
, where it is expected to display new models and further expand its upcoming electric motorcycle lineup.
Whether those new motorcycles can arrive quickly enough to turn around the company’s financial situation remains to be seen.
Electrek’s Take
This is genuinely sad news to see. If there’s any legacy motorcycle manufacturer that deserves to succeed in the electric motorcycle space, it’s Harley-Davidson.
Make all the jokes you want about old dudes in leather jackets riding around on loud, chrome-covered motorcycles. But the fact is that Harley-Davidson was taking electric motorcycles seriously when most other major motorcycle manufacturers were still pretending they didn’t exist.
Harley-Davidson didn’t just dip its toes into electric motorcycles. It dove in headfirst, developing the original LiveWire electric motorcycle
well over a decade ago
and eventually bringing a highly acclaimed production bike to market in 2019. That’s right, Harley-Davidson had a legitimately impressive electric motorcycle on the road before COVID was even a thing. Meanwhile, most of its legacy competitors are only now starting to roll out their first serious electric offerings.
And that’s what makes this so frustrating. Harley-Davidson did the hard part. It invested early, developed excellent technology, received rave reviews, and proved that electric motorcycles could be thrilling, premium machines. But building great motorcycles and building a profitable electric motorcycle business have turned out to be two very different challenges.
The timing is especially unfortunate because I genuinely believe LiveWire’s upcoming S4 Honcho series could be exactly what the company needs. These smaller, significantly more affordable electric motorcycles could finally open LiveWire up to a younger audience that doesn’t have $15,000 to drop on a flagship motorcycle but still wants something fun, stylish, and electric for $5,000.
In many ways, that audience seems like a much more natural fit for LiveWire’s branding and ethos than the premium motorcycle market it has been chasing for years.
I really hope LiveWire can find what it needs to get through this difficult period. After spending more than a decade helping drag the legacy motorcycle industry kicking and screaming into the electric age, it would be a real shame to see the company stumble just as its most promising chapter might be about to begin.

title: The Hydrogen Stream: Finnish researchers increase voltage in alkaline systems to cut costs by 10-15% - pv magazine Global
content: Researchers at Finland’s LUT University have achieved a record voltage of 1,000 V in a series-connected alkaline electrolysis system , aiming to improve the cost efficiency of green hydrogen production. According to the researchers, by increasing voltage, the system reduces current requirements, lowering electrical losses and the costs of power supply and power electronics, which account for approximately one-quarter of a hydrogen plant’s investment costs. According to the researchers, halving these costs could reduce total system investment by around 10% to 15%. The research, conducted using ABB power electronics and electrolyser stacks supplied by Estonia-based Stargate Hydrogen, will now focus on optimising system design, modelling and minimising stray currents to support the scale-up of high-voltage electrolysis. Industrial alkaline electrolysers usually operate at roughly a voltage of 200–400 V. Japan’s Jera and India’s AM Green have signed a binding agreement for the long-term supply of approximately 70,000 metric tons of green ammonia annually over five years, marking a significant step toward establishing an international renewable fuel supply chain for maritime transport. Announced on October 27, the agreement covers supplies from AM Green’s planned ammonia production facility in Kakinada, Andhra Pradesh, which is expected to begin operations in 2028-2029. The ammonia will be transported to Japan and supplied through receiving, storage, and distribution facilities near Jera’s Hekinan thermal power station in Aichi Prefecture. The fuel is intended primarily for ammonia-powered car carriers, with JERA working alongside shipping companies Kawasaki Kisen Kaisha and Nippon Yusen Kabushiki Kaisha to develop dedicated bunkering infrastructure. Separately, seven Japanese companies have agreed to develop an integrated ammonia supply chain in the Chubu region and build and operate four ammonia-fueled car carriers, with the vessels and a dedicated bunkering ship scheduled for completion in 2030. The European Commission launched the T-MED Investment Platform, to mobilise large-scale investment in renewable energy and clean technologies across the Mediterranean. EU support will include up to €4.5 billion in guarantee capacity. Among the selected projects, the Niat and Rasgha Wind Projects in Egypt will bring 500 MW of new onshore wind to the Gulf of Suez, strengthening the renewable base for Egypt’s future hydrogen production through European wind technology. Six researchers from the University of Trieste compared renewable hydrogen imports from Oman with domestic production in Italy, finding that importing hydrogen could be more cost-effective, while local production offers a lower carbon footprint. The research, published in the International Journal of Hydrogen Energy, assesses two supply chains based on proton exchange membrane water electrolysis (PEMWE), including renewable electricity generation, hydrogen liquefaction, storage, transportation, and regasification. The analysis estimates a levelized cost of hydrogen (LCOH) of €7.84/kg for imports from Oman, compared with €10.22/kg for domestic production in Italy. However, the Italian supply chain records lower lifecycle emissions, at 2.26 kg of CO₂ equivalent per kilogram of hydrogen, against 2.62 kg for imports. The engineers said in “ A comparative life-cycle and techno-economic assessment of renewable hydrogen supply chains: Domestic production in Italy and imports from Oman ” that electrolysis is the largest contributor to both emissions and costs, accounting for up to 81% of the carbon footprint and 74.4% of the LCOH. Maritime shipping accounts for around 10% of the imported hydrogen’s final cost. The study also identifies ports and regional initiatives such as the North Adriatic Hydrogen Valley as potential hubs for integrating domestic production and international imports. title: New framework identifies key costs in PV panel recycling - pv magazine Global
content:
Research & Development
Researchers have proposed a decision-support framework for assessing the costs of recycling end-of-life solar panels. An expert panel assigned the highest relative importance to operations and production, followed closely by infrastructure and facilities.
Lior Kahana
30 Oct 2026
Research & Development
Raw Materials
A group of researchers from Brazil’s Pontifical Catholic University of Paraná (PUCPR) has proposed a framework to assess the recycling costs of PV systems, focusing on emerging economies. The framework is based on a literature review and an expert evaluation they conducted.
“This study proposes a structured decision-support framework to support the assessment and management of recycling costs associated with end-of-life photovoltaic panels, with a particular focus on emerging economies,” the group said. “Emerging economies provide the empirical context for developing and validating the proposed framework. Consequently, the category weights and cost prioritization reflect this context, although the framework may be adapted to different regulatory, technological, and market conditions.”
The researchers developed the framework through a systematic literature review, functional cost classification, and expert assessment. Searches in Scopus and Web of Science initially identified 5,784 records, with filtering, duplicate removal, and screening yielding 23 studies explicitly reporting PV recycling costs.
The team extracted 33 cost components and used the Function Analysis System Technique (FAST) to group them into five categories. The first two were infrastructure and facilities (equipment depreciation, collection point operating costs, collection point installation, recycling site installation, and facility investment); and logistics and resources (input storage, transportation, waste collection, auxiliary material acquisition, reverse logistics, and component inventory).
The remaining categories were operations and production (scale, processing, electricity, component handling, component treatment, labor, equipment maintenance, general operating costs, component dismantling, machinery and equipment cleaning, and disposal of non-recoverable parts); management and finance (administrative management, administrative costs, sales costs, material costs, taxes and fees, opportunity costs, indirect economic costs, and financing through bank loans); and sustainability and environmental impacts (external environmental costs, avoided landfill costs, and environmental management costs).
Next, 19 experts rated each component on a five-point importance scale and assessed category relevance from 0% to 100%. The researchers applied the Fuzzy Delphi method to aggregate these judgments and calculate normalized relevance scores, followed by Mean Rank Position analysis to screen borderline components, ultimately retaining 22. The 11 excluded components were input storage, electricity, component handling, equipment maintenance, auxiliary material acquisition, equipment depreciation, administrative management, administrative costs, collection point installation, opportunity costs, and machinery and equipment cleaning.
An adapted Stepwise Weight Assessment Ratio Analysis (SWARA) procedure assigned relative weights to the categories. Finally, the team defined a Costs Index by averaging normalized component values within each category and summing the weighted category scores.
The analysis assigned the highest weight to operations and production (21.71%), followed by infrastructure and facilities (21.48%), logistics and resources (20.11%), sustainability and environmental impacts (18.91%), and management and finance (17.79%). Among the individual components, processing, component treatment, and recycling site installation received the highest normalized relevance scores, at 1.000, 0.882, and 0.836, respectively. Machinery and equipment cleaning and administrative costs received the lowest scores, at 0.039 and 0.000, respectively.
“As its main outcome, the study delivers a structured framework for organizing and assessing photovoltaic panel recycling cost components, providing a consistent basis for comparing technological alternatives, logistics arrangements, suppliers, and regulatory scenarios, thereby supporting strategic planning, operational management, and investment decisions within the photovoltaic circular economy,” the group concluded. “Although developed in the context of an emerging economy, the framework may be adapted to other regional settings by recalibrating cost components and category weights to local conditions.”
The article “
A decision-support framework for structuring and assessing photovoltaic panel recycling costs in emerging economies
” has appeared in the
Journal of Cleaner Production.

title: Stepped air channel, perforated fins improve passive cooling in PVT - pv magazine Global
content:
Research & Development
Researchers have proposed a PV-thermal air collector that combines a stepped channel with perforated V-shaped fins to improve heat dissipation. Simulations showed that the design reduced PV surface temperature by 9 C and reached a maximum thermal efficiency of 31%.
Lior Kahana
30 Oct 2026
Research & Development
Cells & modules
Ilustração de um coletor fotovoltaico-térmico (PVT) com aletas de resfriamento perfuradas.
Researchers from Saudi Arabia and Algeria proposed a novel passive cooling system for PV–thermal (PVT) systems that combines a stepped air channel with perforated fins behind a solar panel. The staircase-shaped air channel is intended to disrupt the insulating air layer that develops along a heated surface. In contrast, the perforated V-shaped fins are intended to increase the heat-transfer area and promote air mixing.
“The system operates entirely under passive, naturally ventilated conditions, with airflow driven by buoyancy forces without auxiliary fans, pumps, or any external energy input for air circulation,” the academics said. “This passive design eliminates parasitic energy consumption and ensures maintenance-free operation, making it particularly suitable for deployment in arid, high-irradiance regions.”
The researchers used ANSYS Fluent to simulate a staircase-configured PVT air collector measuring 2.4 m × 0.54 m and tilted at 32 degrees. It featured a stepped air channel behind the PV module, two air inlets, one outlet, and staggered V-shaped aluminum fins with 5 mm-diameter perforations. Each fin measured 0.17 m long, 0.02 m high, and 0.0045 m thick. A CFD model simulated airflow and heat transfer.
The team applied solar irradiance and ambient temperature data for a clear summer day in Ghardaïa, Algeria, with irradiance peaking at 995 W/m² and temperatures ranging from 306 K to 318 K. After testing five computational meshes, it selected one with approximately 5.51 million elements. The researchers calculated thermal output from the airflow rate and inlet–outlet temperature difference and estimated electrical output using a temperature-dependent PV model.  They compared the design with a reference PVT system.
“The system had a maximum thermal efficiency of 31% (vs. 29.4% for the reference) and electrical efficiency of 14.8% (vs. 14.6%), with peak outputs of 400 W thermal and 180 W electrical, driven by enhanced heat dissipation and turbulence,” the results showed. “It achieved a 9 K reduction in PV surface temperature through passive, naturally ventilated cooling.”
The findings show a 5.8-year payback period under clear-sky conditions and 7.2 years under cloudy conditions. It mitigates 3.2 tons of CO2 per 10-panel system annually, totaling 80 tons over 25 years, with an energy payback time of 0.86 years.
The article “
A computational investigation of a staircase-configured PVT air system with perforated V-shaped fins for passive cooling
” was presented in
Ain Shams Engineering Journal.
Researchers from Saudi Arabia’s
Islamic University of Madinah
, Algeria’s El Oued University, and the
Renewable Energy Development Center
have contributed to the study.

title: Benin secures financing for first solar IPP projects - pv magazine Global
content:

The €30 million ($33.5 million) financing package goes towards the construction and operation of four PV plants forming part of Benin’s first independent power producer solar project.
Patrick Jowett
30 Oct 2026
Applications & Installations
Utility-scale
The Illoulofin solar power plant is currently Benin’s largest operational solar project
Pan-African conglomerate
has entered into a financing agreement for the development of four solar projects with a combined capacity of 62 MW.
The €30 million ($33.5 million) financing package is provided by the
International Finance Corporation
Proparco
, the private sector financing arm of French public development bank Agence Française de Développement. IFC is also mobilizing resources from the Clean Technology Fund, an international fund dedicated to financing clean technologies in developing countries.
The financing goes toward the IPP50 project, which is billed as Benin’s first independent power producer solar project, covering the construction and operation of four solar projects in the cities of Natitingou, Djougou, Parakou and Bohicon, according to a statement published by Axian.
Once operational, the four plants are expected to generate approximately 110 GWh of electricity annually, equivalent to an increase of around 17% in domestic power generation from 2028 to 2035.
The electricity generated will be sold to Benin’s state-owned electric utility Société béninoise de production d’électricité (SBPE) under long-term power purchase agreements. Commercial operations for each of the plants is targeted in the first quarter of 2028.
Total project costs of the IPP50 project, which forms part of a public-private partnership structured around concession agreements granted by the Benin government, are expected to reach €45 million.
Axian’s statement adds the project also contributes to Benin’s National Energy Compact, which is aiming to provide approximately 928,000 additional households with access to electricity by 2030, raise the national electrification rate to at least 70% and increase the share of renewables to 30% of the power generation mix.
Benjamin Memmi, CEO of AXIAN Group’s Energy division, commented that IPP50 “reflects the ambition of the Beninese authorities to accelerate the country’s energy transition, particularly through strong partnerships with the private sector”.
Benin’s largest operational PV project is the Illoulofin solar power plant, according to the Africa Solar Industry Association’s (AFSIA) project database, with a capacity of 50 MW built across two phases.

title: Start of spring in Australia brings stark divides between east and west - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
In a new weekly update for pv magazine,
, a DNV company, reports that Australia’s first month of spring brought above average irradiance to the country’s east, while the west experienced widespread irradiance deficits.
30 Oct 2026
Markets & Policy
Asia-Pacific
Utility-scale
Australia’s first month of spring brought a strong east-west divide in solar irradiance and precipitation, while temperatures were above average across most of the country, according to analysis using the
Solcast API
. Eastern Australia experienced generally above average irradiance and unusually dry conditions, with the strongest irradiance increases occurring inland rather than along the coast. In contrast, remote mining solar projects in Western Australia’s Pilbara and Goldfields-Esperance regions experienced widespread irradiance deficits, as slow-moving weather systems brought increased cloud cover and rainfall.
Across eastern Australia, September irradiance averaged 5% above normal. Coastal locations, including most distributed PV markets, generally remained within a few percent of average, while areas further inland hosting utility-scale PV recorded increases of around 10%. Parts of Tasmania experienced near-record or record September irradiance for the Solcast data period, averaging 10% above normal. These conditions coincided with exceptionally dry weather across the southeast, with rainfall deficits exceeding 30 mm across much of New South Wales, Victoria and Tasmania. Most locations in these states experienced record or near-record September dryness, continuing the below-average rainfall conditions observed through winter.
Western Australia experienced contrasting conditions, with September irradiance averaging 11% below normal. The Pilbara recorded irradiance around 10% below average, while the Goldfields Esperance region experienced larger deficits of 15–20%. Further inland, parts of the Gibson Desert recorded irradiance as much as 29% below average.
Several slow-moving low-pressure systems brought persistent cloud cover to inland Western Australia, contributing to the region’s below-average irradiance. The most significant rainfall occurred between September 5 and 9, when large parts of Goldfields Esperance received more than 50 mm of rain, compared with a typical September total of just 10 mm.
Despite the reduced irradiance and increased rainfall, temperatures across much of Western Australia remained above average, with parts of the Pilbara exceeding 3°C above normal. Eastern Australia experienced a different combination of conditions, with above average irradiance, unusually dry weather and temperatures generally 1–3°C above average across the southeast.

AI/ML algorithms
. This data is used to drive irradiance models, enabling Solcast to calculate irradiance at high resolution, with typical bias of less than 2%, and also cloud-tracking forecasts. This data is used by more than 350 companies managing over 350 GW of solar assets globally.

title: SEG Solar plans 4 GW HJT cell manufacturing plant in Texas - pv magazine Global
content:
Technology & Products
SEG Solar has secured land for a planned $950 million heterojunction (HJT) solar cell manufacturing facility in the Houston area, Texas.
Ryan Kennedy
30 Oct 2026
Technology & Products
Manufacturing
EG Solar
secured land
for a planned $950 million, 4 GW heterojunction (HJT) solar cell plant at its Tomball Industrial Campus in the greater Houston area.
The multi-phase development is expected to create more than 700 local jobs and is scheduled to come online in two 2 GW phases, targeted for 2028 and 2029.
The cell plant will sit directly adjacent to SEG’s operational 4 GW Tomball #1 module facility and its 4.6 GW Tomball #2 module facility, which is currently under construction. Co-locating the cell lines will bring cell, module, and balance of module production together in one location alongside warehousing, a research and development center, a certified testing laboratory, and planned EVA film and junction box manufacturing lines.
The announcement represents the next step in the company’s domestic vertical integration strategy. Earlier this year, SEG
its Tomball #1 assembly facility, scaling up crystalline-silicon production in Texas as part of a push to build out domestic supply capacity.
Following the site opening, the manufacturer
launched
production of its first commercial-scale HJT modules at the secondary facility, establishing the high-efficiency technology as a central component of its U.S. manufacturing footprint.
Supplying Texas-assembled modules with domestic HJT cells will allow project developers and asset owners to meet federal domestic content requirements under the Inflation Reduction Act while securing dedicated supply chains.
“Bringing HJT cell manufacturing to the U.S. will give customers a more domestic supply chain with clearer sourcing and a single company standing behind the product,” said Jim Wood, chief executive officer of SEG Solar, who recently
on U.S. manufacturing expansion at
pv magazine USA Week 2026
. “As the only U.S. company dedicated to integrated domestic vertical manufacturing, SEG will continue to strengthen our U.S. operations and innovation.”
Founded in 2021, the Houston-headquartered manufacturer reported shipping over 7.5 GW of solar modules globally through the end of 2025, reaching an annual module production capacity of 6.5 GW.
