title: China polysilicon prices hold amid market standoff, spot-futures gap - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
In a new weekly update for
pv magazine
, OPIS, a Dow Jones company, provides a quick look at the main price trends in the global PV industry.
30 Oct 2026
Markets & Policy
The China Mono Premium, the OPIS assessment for mono-grade polysilicon used in n-type ingot production, was unchanged at CNY 38.786 ($5.82)/kg, or CNY 0.081/W, according to the OPIS Global Solar Markets Report released on Oct. 27.
According to market participants, the fundamentals of the Chinese polysilicon market remain unchanged, with the market continuing to be characterized by manufacturers holding firm to full-cost-based offers while downstream buyers show limited willingness to accept current prices. This has kept prices largely at a standstill, with inventory levels exceeding 500,000 metric tons (MT) further prolonging the impasse.
Industry participants widely noted that futures prices, which remain significantly below mainstream spot prices, have provided a degree of balance to the ongoing standoff between upstream suppliers and downstream buyers. According to data from the Guangzhou Futures Exchange on Oct. 26, settlement prices for polysilicon futures contracts for delivery between November 2026 and October 2027 ranged from a low of CNY 33.620/kg to a high of CNY 37.180/kg, with even the highest about 4.14% below the latest spot assessment.
Market participants explained that actual spot transactions continue to be concluded at higher prices than futures contracts, partly because customers with long-term purchase agreements still need to procure some material in the spot market. To offset the higher procurement costs, these buyers also source relatively lower-priced polysilicon from futures traders, helping to balance their overall purchasing costs.
One trade participant said that futures traders had been gradually selling off previously accumulated stocks of low-priced polysilicon into the spot market. However, the availability of this lower-priced material is expected to diminish over time. The participant added that manufacturers adhering to the industry self-discipline agreement appear determined not to sell polysilicon at prices below CNY 40/kg during the fourth quarter. As low-priced supplies dwindle and manufacturers maintain their price stance, futures prices are expected to gradually rise, allowing actual spot transaction prices to find a new balance between futures prices and prevailing spot offers.
Separately, an industry source said the China Photovoltaic Industry Association would organize monitoring activities to oversee the implementation of polysilicon production cuts planned for the fourth quarter, adding that this gives the market a degree of confidence and expectation that prices will remain stable. However, no official confirmation or disclosure regarding these activities was available at the time of reporting.
Looking ahead, an upstream participant expected mainstream polysilicon offers to remain unchanged until the Lunar New Year in early February 2027. Meanwhile, prices offered by manufacturers that have not signed the pricing self-discipline agreement, along with polysilicon futures prices, are expected to remain below mainstream spot offers.
The Global Polysilicon Marker (GPM), the benchmark for polysilicon produced outside China, was assessed at $19.234/kg, or $0.040/W, unchanged from the previous week.
Both manufacturers and buyers in the global polysilicon market continued to face mounting pressure. One trade participant noted that some suppliers had reduced their China-based polysilicon sales teams to just a handful of people, underscoring the increasingly weak demand environment.
On the demand side, a source at an integrated manufacturer said that certain long-term contract holders with cell manufacturing facilities in the U.S. could still absorb around 300 MT of global polysilicon per month. While this volume provides some support for demand, the contribution remains relatively small and limited in scope.
Certain long-term contract holders, despite being in poor financial condition, reportedly continue to purchase global polysilicon at a loss due to their contractual obligations. However, the pricing mechanisms embedded in long-term contracts negotiated several years ago have given buyers some room to negotiate, potentially allowing these agreements to remain in effect despite challenging market conditions.
In the near term, industry participants generally expect the main sources of global polysilicon supply to remain U.S.-produced material and lower-priced polysilicon from other origins. In addition, the framework established under the Section 232 outcome has enabled limited volumes of compliant Chinese polysilicon to continue flowing into Southeast Asia.
OPIS, a Dow Jones company, provides energy prices, news, data, and analysis on gasoline, diesel, jet fuel, LPG/NGL, coal, metals, and chemicals, as well as renewable fuels and environmental commodities. It acquired pricing data assets from Singapore Solar Exchange in 2022 and now publishes the
OPIS APAC Solar Weekly Report

title: US top rival could begin space war using low orbit laser weapons
content: A new report released by the United States has revealed that China could deploy laser weapons in space before 2030. The report released by Defense Intelligence Agency stated that China, Russia, Iran, and North Korea are developing, testing, deploying, and using space capabilities in a way that threatens the security of all space systems and their associated space benefits. Safe, secure, and sustainable space domainTitled Challenges to Security in Space, the report claimed that China and Russia are developing a formidable spectrum of offensive capabilities to degrade or destroy space services of other countries, from kinetic destruction to sophisticated jamming and cyber operations. These countries have exhibited behaviors that often run counter to a safe, secure, and sustainable space domain.Counterspace weapons can deny, jam, temporarily disable, or permanently incapacitate space assets, along with the vital services they provide. Military, civil, and commercial providers deliver space services that collectively can be held at risk by an actor with the intent to interfere with military space services, since commercial and civil space services sometimes have connections to certain military capabilities. Although many counterspace weapons or tactics are intended to degrade space services temporarily, others can damage or destroy satellites permanently, according to the report.Antisatellite (ASAT) missiles are designed to kinetically strike and destroy satellites. ASAT missiles could produce massive amounts of debris that can remain in orbit for decades or even centuries.Critical component to conduct modern “informatized warfare”The report also highlighted that PLA’s objectives include space dominance as Beijing has ability to control the space-enabled information sphere and deny its adversaries their own spacebased information gathering and communications capabilities. China views space dominance as a critical component to conduct modern “informatized warfare.”China has developed and will continue to advance weapons for use against satellites in orbit to disrupt, damage, and destroy other nations’ space capabilities.113,114 China continues to research, develop, test, and deploy multiple types of counterspace weapons, including ground-based ASAT missile systems capable of destroying satellites.Directed-energy weapons (DEWs) can temporarily or permanently blind imagery satellites and affect overhead persistent infrared (OPIR) and weather sensors, thereby denying the ability to monitor, track, and target forces.It’s also claimed that countries with nuclear weapons can launch a warhead on a long-range booster, such as an intercontinental ballistic missile (ICBM) or space launch vehicle (SLV), and probably conduct a high-altitude nuclear detonation, or even place a nuclear weapon in space. In either case, a nuclear detonation in or near space would create widespread electromagnetic disruptions in space and on Earth, leading to potential damage or destruction of satellites.China is developing space launch capabilities to ensure it has an independent, reliable means to access space and to compete in the international space launch market. Beijing set a national record for space launches in 2025 with 93, including 25 commercial launches. There already have been 18 launches in the first quarter of 2026, with 6 being commercial launches.254 China is working to improve manufacturing efficiencies and launch capabilities, while trying to expand its human spaceflight and deep-space exploration missions, including to the Moon and Mars.China is developing space-based technology, including on-orbit counterspace weapons, capable of holding space systems at risk. To research space debris cleanup, China has launched multiple satellites, such as the Shijian-21 in GEO, to conduct scientific experiments and test space maintenance technologies. Such systems, including the Shijian-17, a satellite with a robotic arm, can be used for grappling other satellites. In January 2022, Shijian-21 moved a derelict BeiDou navigation satellite to a high graveyard orbit above GEO. In January 2025, China launched the Shijian-25 in GEO, which it claims will test orbital refueling and servicing capabilities.The report also underlined that China has multiple ground-based laser weapons with varying power levels to disrupt, degrade, or damage satellites in LEO. By the late 2020s, China may field space-based directed energy systems and higher-powered ground-based directed energy systems capable of threatening satellites in higher orbits. In January 2021, PLA media asserted that laser weapons were entering a golden age; they cited dazzling (i.e., temporarily blinding a sensor) as one of the many operational uses of laser weapons.

title: China tests smart nuclear submarine operation at 23,000 feet depth
content: China has tested upgraded AI systems during deep-sea trials of its Jiaolong crewed submersible, demonstrating technology that could eventually support military submarine operations.The trials took place in the Philippine Basin in the western Pacific Ocean, where the submersible reached a depth of 7,056.9 meters (23,000 feet).The upgrades include AI-powered seabed analysis and a fault-diagnosis system designed to assist pilots during underwater operations.The technology could also help improve decision-making and emergency responses aboard nuclear-powered submarines.China tests submarine AIChina has demonstrated AI technology during deep-sea trials of its upgraded Jiaolong crewed submersible, highlighting systems that could eventually support decision-making and emergency responses aboard nuclear-powered submarines.According to Chinese media reports, the trials followed a major upgrade that introduced AI-powered seabed analysis and a separate fault-diagnosis system to assist pilots during underwater operations.The latest development highlighted AI’s potential to support complex underwater missions, where limited communication with the outside world makes autonomous analysis and rapid decision-making particularly important.One of Jiaolong’s upgrades is a fault-diagnosis and decision-support system designed to help pilots identify equipment problems and respond to malfunctions during dives. When a fault occurs, the system provides troubleshooting procedures, records of previous failures and relevant technical documents. It covers critical equipment, including propulsion and control systems, helping pilots identify potential problems and determine appropriate responses.The technology is designed to speed up fault identification and help crews address equipment issues before they develop into more serious problems. Such capabilities could be useful aboard nuclear-powered submarines undertaking prolonged underwater missions. Equipment failures in these environments require immediate attention, particularly when crews have limited access to external technical support. AI-based predictive maintenance could also help identify abnormal operating conditions and potential component failures before they cause equipment breakdowns.Submarines face additional challenges because they cannot depend on continuous satellite communications while submerged. AI-assisted systems could help crews process information, assess equipment conditions and make decisions with limited external support. Jiaolong has also received an intelligent exploration system developed using a multimodal large AI model. The technology analyses images captured by the submersible’s cameras to identify marine organisms and seabed materials.Deep-sea explorationResearchers trained the system using more than 800,000 images of deep-sea organisms and underwater materials. It can interpret camera footage in real time and automatically record identified objects alongside their geographical coordinates, observation times and diving depths.The system also supports manual corrections when it misidentifies objects. Researchers can feed these corrections back into the model to improve its recognition capabilities. Users can interact with the software through dialogue to obtain information about underwater observations. It can also reconstruct the submersible’s diving trajectory in three dimensions, analyze marine species abundance and generate reports on seabed ecosystems.Although developed primarily for scientific exploration, similar AI techniques could potentially be adapted for underwater military operations. For instance, specialized models could be trained to analyze acoustic data collected by submarine sonar systems. These systems receive signals from vessels, marine life and surrounding underwater environments, making accurate classification important for identifying potential threats.According to experts, AI could help distinguish between different sources of underwater noise and flag unusual acoustic patterns for human operators. However, Jiaolong’s current exploration system focuses on visual analysis rather than military sonar-based target recognition. The specific depths at which its AI systems were tested were also not disclosed.The latest trials additionally verified the reliability of Jiaolong’s upgraded equipment, including key components replaced with domestically developed alternatives.

title: US sends first home-built centrifuge for advanced nuclear reactors
content: An American nuclear fuel supplier, Centrus Energy, has completed its Oak Ridge plant and is shipping the first new centrifuge to its Ohio facility as part of the company’s expansion of its uranium enrichment capacity.​The centrifuges produced in Tennessee will now be grouped into ‘cascades’ and integrated into the uranium enrichment facility in Ohio, the company announced Thursday. The energy firm said in a statement that the new capacity is expected to ‘come online’ in 2029.​A cascade is a group of centrifuges connected together to enrich uranium, as multiple centrifuges are needed to achieve the required enrichment level. The Ohio facility has an existing cascade of these centrifuges, which includes components built nearly seven years ago.Uranium for next-gen reactors​At the expanded facility, Centrus aims to produce Low-Enriched Uranium (LEU) on a large scale “for the existing reactor fleet for baseload electricity, High-Assay Low-Enriched Uranium (HALEU) for next-generation reactors, and enrichment for national security needs.”​HALEU has enriched uranium of 5-20 percent, while LEU has generally 3-5 percent for conventional reactors.​Centrus described the centrifuge shipment as a “milestone” which was achieved ahead of its previously announced target.​It also said that it contracted a network of domestic suppliers to establish a supply chain capable of meeting both commercial and national security demand.​To secure the supply chain, the company completed the acquisition of Westerman Holdings earlier in October.​Westerman Holdings is a key supplier of centrifuge casings and other major components.​”Completing the first new centrifuge for our expansion and standing up a one-of-a-kind supply chain are significant moments for our team and this country,” Centrus president and Chief Executive Officer Amir Vexler said.​”Building this unique manufacturing capability at scale takes specialized expertise, time, precision and sustained commitment. These milestones demonstrate our ability to translate our investment into tangible progress and position us to re-establish this country’s rightful position in the global enrichment market,” he added.Boost to domestic manufacturingIn December 2025, the nuclear supplier restarted centrifuge manufacturing activities in Oak Ridge to expand enrichment capacity in Ohio.​The following month, in January 2026, the energy corporation announced a $560 million investment to expand and modernize the centrifuge facility in Oak Ridge.​A centrifuge plays a crucial role in a uranium enrichment plant. It uses uranium hexafluoride gas (UF6) and rotates it at high speeds to increase the concentration of uranium-235 (U-235) relative to uranium-238 (U-238), as natural uranium contains approximately 0.7 percent U-235. The U-235 isotope is used to sustain a nuclear chain reaction.​Currently, Centrus’s existing centrifuge cascade in Ohio has components manufactured in 2019, with some also being older than that. And it has been producing High-Assay, Low-Enriched Uranium (HALEU) since late 2023.​Tennessee Governor Bill Lee hailed the shipment, calling it “an important milestone in strengthening America’s nuclear fuel supply chain”, while Senator Bill Hagerty said, “We’re turning decades of investment and expertise into American manufacturing, American energy, and American opportunity.” ​According to Centrus, the Oak Ridge facility is the only advanced centrifuge manufacturing plant in the US with a proven and de-risked technology, while “all other centrifuge technologies in commercial operation today are manufactured exclusively overseas.”

title: Rheinmetall to supply anti-tank missile firing Schakal infantry vehicles
content: Germany and the Netherlands have expanded their joint armored vehicle program by ordering 69 additional Schakal infantry fighting vehicles.The Organization for Joint Armament Cooperation (OCCAR) has commissioned Artec GmbH, a joint venture between Rheinmetall and KNDS Deutschland. It will supply 35 vehicles for the German Bundeswehr and 34 for the Dutch armed forces. The two option call-offs have a combined value in the medium three-digit million-euro range, according to Rheinmetall.Deliveries are scheduled between May 2032 and November 2033. The latest order follows the first option call-off under the program, which received approval from Germany’s Bundestag Budget Committee on June 24, 2026. With the new vehicles included, the number of Schakals ordered for delivery now stands at 291.Boxer chassis meets Puma firepowerThe Schakal combines two established German armored vehicle platforms: the wheeled Boxer 8×8 chassis and the turret of the tracked Puma infantry fighting vehicle. The configuration brings the mobility and modular design of the Boxer together with the Puma’s weapons system, creating a vehicle intended to support mechanized infantry operations.Its primary weapon is the Rheinmetall MK 30-2/ABM 30 mm automatic cannon, supplemented by a MELLS anti-tank guided missile system. The combination gives the vehicle options for engaging a range of battlefield threats, from lighter armored vehicles to more heavily protected targets. It is also designed to carry a fully equipped infantry squad, allowing troops to travel with the vehicle and dismount when required.The Boxer platform is built around a modular architecture, allowing different mission configurations to share a common vehicle base. Its eight-wheel drive configuration is intended to provide the mobility medium forces need for long-distance operations, while offering a different approach to deployment and transport than heavier tracked vehicles.Expanding German-Dutch armored vehicle cooperationThe latest order builds on the original contract awarded to Artec in October 2025, which covered 222 Schakal vehicles and included options for up to 200 additional units. The first option exercise and the latest call-off have steadily expanded the program beyond its initial order.The project is also part of a broader effort to strengthen cooperation between European defense industries and standardize equipment across allied forces. Alongside Rheinmetall and KNDS Deutschland, the program involves industrial partners including MTU and Hensoldt, as well as small and medium-sized enterprises.For Germany and the Netherlands, operating the same vehicle could support closer coordination in training, maintenance, logistics, and joint deployments. Shared platforms can also help reduce the complexity of supporting different vehicle types across allied units.Rheinmetall says German industry has guaranteed accelerated deliveries for vehicles covered by the options. The company has also identified a potential role for the Schakal in the proposed Arminius Boxer program, should it receive a formal commission.The additional order reinforces the two countries’ commitment to the platform, although the bulk of the newly ordered vehicles will not arrive until the next decade. With deliveries extending into 2033, the program represents a long-term investment in wheeled infantry fighting vehicles and closer German-Dutch military cooperation.

title: Germany and Ukraine test armed ground robot with machine gun and grenade launcher
content: German defense technology company ARX Robotics and Ukrainian firm ROBONEERS have completed initial integration tests of an armed uncrewed ground vehicle (UGV) designed for frontline operations in Ukraine. The system combines ARX’s GEREON robotic vehicle with ROBONEERS’ remotely operated SABER weapons module. The companies expect to deliver the first equipped units to Ukrainian forces by the end of 2026.Announced on October 29, the demonstration marks a new phase in the two companies’ defense cooperation, which signed a partnership agreement in Kyiv earlier this month during German Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s visit to Ukraine. The agreement was signed in the presence of Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.The combined platform is designed to provide remotely operated fire support and will allow soldiers to control the vehicle from a safer distance.GEREON platform combines mobility and firepowerDeveloped by ARX Robotics, GEREON is a modular uncrewed ground vehicle designed to perform different military missions. It provides the mobility, onboard power, and sensor capabilities. On the other hand, the SABER module developed by ROBONEERS adds remotely operated weapons.The initial integration involves two SABER configurations: M2, equipped with a .50-caliber M2 heavy machine gun, and MK 19 (M), which uses a 40 mm automatic grenade launcher, according to Defense Blog. The SABER module is designed as a remotely operated weapon station, allowing personnel to control its functions without being physically positioned alongside the vehicle. Combined with GEREON’s cameras and sensors, the system can support reconnaissance and combat operations while reducing soldiers’ exposure to direct fire.According to ARX Robotics, the integration allows the vehicle and weapons module to operate as a single mission system, with the first M2 and MK 19 (M) configurations scheduled for integration by the end of 2026.Ground robots take on more frontline missionsThe GEREON platform is already being used in Ukraine in unarmed configurations for tasks such as transporting supplies, evacuating wounded personnel, reconnaissance, and electronic warfare. Its modular architecture lets the same vehicle family adapt be different operational requirements, rather than relying on separate platforms for every mission.The addition of SABER extends those applications to armed support. Depending on its configuration, the vehicle could provide remotely operated fire support while keeping troops farther from exposed positions.ARX Robotics describes GEREON as the largest fleet of Western-built uncrewed ground vehicles currently deployed in Ukraine. ROBONEERS, meanwhile, says its robotic systems have supported more than 15,000 frontline missions since 2014.The development reflects Ukraine’s growing use of ground robots for missions that would otherwise expose soldiers to artillery, small-arms fire, and drone attacks. Beyond carrying supplies and evacuating casualties, armed UGVs offer another way to provide support in areas where deploying personnel directly can be particularly dangerous.Germany and Ukraine expand robotics cooperationThe GEREON-SABER integration is part of a broader industrial partnership between the German and Ukrainian companies. ARX Robotics and ROBONEERS have also established a joint venture, ARX Industries, to expand production of another uncrewed ground vehicle, the Rys Pro, in Germany and Ukraine.The companies are targeting production of more than 1,000 Rys Pro vehicles during its first year, reflecting their ambition to scale robotic systems for military use.For the GEREON-SABER configuration, the immediate next step is integrating the first weapons modules and delivering the vehicles according to the operational requirements of Ukraine’s armed forces.

title: US Navy boosts Northrop Grumman's bomb fuze production plant
content: The U.S. Navy is increasing the maximum value of an existing Northrop Grumman contract by approximately $97 million to support continued production of the FMU-139D/B electronic bomb fuze, the company announced October 29.The device controls when and how a munition functions and is used on numerous U.S. and allied aircraft and various munitions. Production takes place at the Naval Industrial Reserve Ordnance Plant at Allegany Ballistics Laboratory in Rocket Center, West Virginia.The contract increase extends manufacturing of the system as demand for munitions grows. Northrop said investments in automation and advanced manufacturing have expanded the facility’s capacity to as many as 85,000 fuzes annually.Electronic safety and timingThe FMU-139D/B is a safety and timing device designed to help ensure that munitions function as intended. Northrop describes the fuze as adaptable and operationally proven, with applications across different aircraft and weapons.The company said the system supports U.S. and allied forces in maintaining ready, reliable stockpiles. Its continued production contributes to the availability of a component used in the U.S. military’s inventory of air-delivered weapons.The latest contract action supports further production of the existing fuze at the West Virginia facility, where Northrop has maintained a longstanding manufacturing effort.Production reaches delivery milestoneEarlier this year, Northrop delivered its 200,000th FMU-139D/B fuze, marking a milestone for the program. The company cited that delivery as evidence of its ability to manufacture the system at scale.At Allegany Ballistics Laboratory, investments in automation and advanced manufacturing technologies have increased efficiency and expanded production capacity, according to Northrop.Those improvements allow the facility to produce as many as 85,000 fuzes a year. The company said they have also strengthened its ability to respond quickly during periods of increased demand.The approximately $97 million increase in the contract’s maximum value supports continued production of the fuze at the same facility.Fuze and warhead manufacturingThe FMU-139D/B is part of Northrop’s broader portfolio of fuzing and warhead technologies. The company develops these systems to provide precise, reliable effects tailored to different missions and operational environments.Northrop said its campus combines capabilities in metals, electronics, composites and energetics. It describes itself as the only company bringing all four capabilities together at a single campus.That combination supports integrated fuze and warhead design, alongside the development of adaptable systems optimized for performance, survivability, manufacturability and scalable production.The company said these capabilities support current military missions, while the latest Navy contract increase extends production of the FMU-139D/B.The delivery milestone and annual manufacturing capacity describe different aspects of the program. The 200,000th fuze represents a cumulative delivery milestone, while the 85,000 figure describes how many fuzes the facility can now manufacture annually. Northrop attributes the expanded capacity to investments in automation and advanced manufacturing technologies, which it says have improved efficiency and strengthened the plant’s ability to respond quickly during periods of increased demand for these systems.

title: Rolls-Royce to develop next-gen jet engines for efficient flights
content: Cleaner, more efficient jet engines for single-aisle passenger aircraft are the focus of a $3.3 billion (£2.5 billion) program agreed between the UK government and Rolls-Royce, with joint funding spread over 10 years.Announced on October 28 alongside the Budget, the agreement aims to develop jet engine technologies and sustain British aerospace manufacturing over the coming decades.The investment is expected to support 3,300 existing jobs over the next few years, with the potential to create tens of thousands of additional roles in the longer term.Rolls-Royce estimates that securing a UK engine for the single-aisle aircraft market could attract billions of pounds in further investment and add $161 billion (£120 billion) to the economy over the program’s lifetime.Those figures remain projections tied to securing that market opportunity.Targeting single-aisle aircraftThe program will focus on jet engines for single-aisle aircraft, the passenger planes commonly used on routes between Britain and European destinations.The government’s Industrial Strategy identifies this market as the UK aerospace sector’s biggest opportunity over the next 50 years. The agreement seeks to position British industry to compete for that demand while maintaining the capabilities needed to develop and manufacture commercial aircraft engines.“This is a landmark moment for the UK’s aerospace industry. This is a once-in-a-generation opportunity to lay the foundations for decades of sustainable economic growth across the UK, creating high-value jobs and transforming the country’s advanced manufacturing supply chain,” said Rolls-Royce chief executive Tufan Erginbilgic.The cooperation extends beyond the initial funding period, with the government describing it as a multi-decade agreement intended to encourage sustained industrial investment.Materials, robotics and AI to help develop the jet engineTechnology development will include advanced materials, electronic systems, advanced manufacturing, robotics and artificial intelligence.These areas form part of the effort to develop cleaner and more efficient jet engines. The announcement does not provide specific fuel-efficiency targets, emissions reductions or a date for an engine to enter service.The engineering skills and industrial capabilities developed through the agreement could also support military aircraft engines, giving the program potential applications across both civil and defense aerospace.“Aerospace is a growing and globally attractive market, and this program with Government is vital to enable the UK to compete,” Erginbilgic said.The agreement also includes a jobs and skills plan intended to develop the workforce needed for future aerospace activity, alongside the investment in technology and manufacturing capabilities.Jobs across the supply chainPotential new roles would span engineering, research and manufacturing, covering work from initial design through to factory production.The government expects the vast majority of those positions to be created outside London and the South East, drawing on Rolls-Royce’s existing sites and supply chains across the country.A central commitment is to work with Rolls-Royce, the wider aerospace industry and regional and local expertise to ensure UK-based suppliers benefit from sustained investment.The agreement aims to create opportunities for businesses to start, expand and export British expertise. Its longer-term economic and employment benefits will depend on the program’s progress and the UK’s ability to secure a place in the future single-aisle engine market.

title: NASA scientists identify 4.1-billion-year-old rock from Mars crust
content: When nomadic prospectors stumbled across a curious rose-tinted rock scattered across Mali’s desolate salt plains in 2022, they had no idea they were holding a lost piece of planetary history.It was nearly ignored. Researchers initially suspected the 800-gram (2-pound) specimen was just another common shergottite — a familiar class among the roughly 435 Martian rocks that have crashed into Earth. And now, it turns out the experts were initially wrong. In a new study, NASA-funded researchers revealed that the meteorite, dubbed Teghaza 001, is actually a 4.1-billion-year-old fragment of the primordial Martian crust. The discovery makes it one of the absolute oldest rocks from the Red Planet ever identified, offering humanity a rare glance back to a time when Mars looked like Earth.Mineral and isotopic analyses reveal that subsurface water altered the rock around 4.1 billion years ago, pointing to a far more dynamic early Martian water cycle than previously understood.Scientists identified 13 locations on Mars that match the mineralogy and chemistry of Teghaza 001, one of the most ancient Martian meteorites ever found on Earth. Credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech/USGSEvidence of ancient waterWhat makes the meteorite remarkable is not just its age, but what happened to it.Teghaza 001 sets itself apart from rare peers like ALH84001 and “Black Beauty” through its complex, multi-mineral volcanic structure rather than a single mineral or fragmented composition.“It was only after we started looking closely that we realized this meteorite is really unique. One of the paper’s reviewers called it a Rosetta Stone for Mars,” said Yang Liu of NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Southern California.Unlocking the rock’s secrets required precision techniques that seem pulled from science fiction.To date the sample without destroying it, Caltech geochemist Francois Tissot applied a precise rubidium-strontium method directly to the rock’s surface. Most of the age-dating methods dissolve an entire specimen in acid, but this advanced approach preserved the rare Martian sample. The team targeted microscopic zircon grains across a tiny patch smaller than a fingernail, achieving accurate results while keeping the meteorite intact for future research.The results shocked the lab. The chemical signatures confirmed that a dynamic, active water cycle altered Martian geology 4.1 billion years ago. It was the time when the planet began losing its ancient atmosphere to space.“This is really our first piece of Martian crust from a part of Mars we’ve never had a sample of before. It records interactions of water and rock and maybe even an imprint of the Martian atmosphere as it was losing water,” said Lee Saper, the new paper’s second author.Part of Mars’ highlandsScientists cross-referenced Teghaza 001’s mineral signature with remote sensing data from NASA’s Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter, indicating its chemical twin in the heavily cratered southern highlands of Mars.Somewhere in those ancient hills, a violent cosmic collision blasted the rock into space. The blast sent the rock on an interplanetary journey that ended thousands of millennia later in the sands of the Sahara.Now safe in university vaults, the rose-colored stranger is forcing geologists to rethink how quickly Mars cooled, formed continents, and dried up. As Liu put it: “We’ve only scratched the surface.”The study findings were published in the journal Science.

title: 10,000-ton US attack submarines to get new Northrop Grumman generators
content: Northrop Grumman has finalized an order to supply propulsion machinery and onboard power generators for 12 additional Virginia-class Block VI submarine shipsets, extending its work on the Navy program through 2032.The $1.4 billion contract covers main propulsion units and ship service turbine generators, Chief Executive Kathy Warden told analysts during the company’s October 20 earnings call.In a separate contract, the Navy contracted Northrop to produce AN/WSN-12 inertial navigation systems, which use fiber-optic gyroscopes to help ships and submarines determine their position and motion when GPS is unavailable or unreliable. The initial contract is worth $29.2 million, with options that could raise its value to $103.6 million.Propulsion and onboard powerThe Virginia-class procurement covers two equipment categories with distinct roles: main propulsion units for driving the submarines and ship service turbine generators for supplying onboard electrical power.“We also definitized the Virginia-class Block VI submarine procurement for an additional 12 shipsets of main propulsion units and ship service turbine generators,” Warden said. “The award value adds $1.4 billion to backlog, supporting our partnership with the Navy through 2032,” he said.The announcement concerns equipment procurement for the submarine program. It does not establish delivery dates for individual vessels or describe changes to propulsion performance.Chief Financial Officer John Greene said higher marine systems volumes helped lift third-quarter sales at Northrop’s Mission Systems division by 2%. Increased activity on restricted airborne radar programs also contributed.Navigation without continuous GPSThe separate AN/WSN-12 award addresses a different operational requirement: maintaining navigation information without continuously relying on external positioning signals.Inertial navigation systems use gyroscopes and accelerometers to measure motion and calculate navigation information from an initial position. The AN/WSN-12 packages this capability into an Inertial Sensor Module and a Navigation Processor Module.Its central technology change is the use of fiber-optic gyroscopes instead of the ring-laser gyroscopes found in the legacy AN/WSN-7.The Navy describes the replacement as compatible in form, fit, and function with the older system, allowing installation on existing vessels as well as new construction. Its navigation output can also feed other shipboard systems that require accurate position, velocity, and attitude data. Acquisition plans call for deployment across surface ships, submarines, and aircraft carriers.Production and fleet upgradesThe navigation contract could reach $103.6 million if all options are exercised. It combines purchases for the Navy, accounting for 27%, with Canada at 42% and Australia at 31% through the Foreign Military Sales program.Work will take place primarily in Charlottesville, Virginia, with the remainder in Baltimore. Completion is expected by May 2030, extending through July 2032 if all options are exercised.A separate planned full-rate production effort covers additional hardware, engineering support, training, testing, and spares. That effort would support new-construction vessels, fleet retrofits, and foreign military deliveries from fiscal 2031 through fiscal 2036.Together, the awards span submarine machinery and fleet navigation. Their schedules and procurement scopes remain separate, covering propulsion equipment on one side and navigation production, integration, testing, and support on the other.

title: New catalytic process recovers 99% of silicone from waste at 176°F
content: Technische Universität Berlin has developed a new catalytic process to fully break down silicone waste.Common items like the silicone spatula in your mixing bowl, the leak-proof seal in your travel mug, and the soft pacifier that keeps a toddler quiet all share a hidden downside. All are immortal.Silicones resist heat, water, and chemical breakdown. Hence, throwing the waste away usually means sending it to a landfill or an incinerator. Until now, a closed-loop recycling has been a tough task, chemically. TU Berlin says they have found a way forward after years of research. Led by Professor Dr. Martin Oestreich, the team developed a catalytic process that breaks down silicon-oxygen polymers back into their original, high-value building block: dimethyldichlorosilane. The study details a strategy that gives up to a 99% recovery rate from regular items like muffin pans and baby bottles. “Our success is proof that basic research can eventually pay off in very specific applications that no one had previously thought of,” said Oestreich. “We’ve been conducting research on silylium ions for 15 years, and it’s only in the last five years or so that we have suddenly identified the recycling of silicones as a key application for this research.”Breaking the bad siliconeThe discovery simply solves a tough chemical problem.To make fresh silicone from scratch, manufacturers first extract raw silicon from quartz sand inside electric arc furnaces fired at extreme temperatures. It is a massive, energy-intensive undertaking. Once formed, the resulting silicon-oxygen bonds behave like molecular superglue. Breaking them requires immense energy or unprecedented catalytic precision.Oestreich’s team spent 15 years studying the silylium ions (positively charged silicon ions) before realizing the hidden potential for waste management. As per the study paper, a new silylium-ion-initiated depolymerization strategy has been developed to enable the sustainable circular recycling of chemically inert silicone (siloxane) materials. When paired with triphosgene — a manageable solid reagent  —the silylium ion strips away a chloride ion to generate a hyper-reactive species known as a chlorocarbonyl cation (COCl+). This molecular scissors snip the silicon-oxygen chain.As the bonds snap apart, the oxygen escapes cleanly into the air as carbon dioxide gas (CO2), preventing the reaction from reversing. The entire sequence runs at a gentle 80°C, requiring negligible energy compared to primary production.Growing silicone waste crisisTesting on items like cupcake pans and lids demonstrated promise. Under moderate conditions at 80°C (176°F), the low-energy process recovered up to 99 percent of dimethyldichlorosilane from individual items within 24 hours. Even when applied to a mixed batch of diverse silicone waste, the method maintained a 86 percent recovery rate.The market for silicone products is continuously growing. It was around USD 19.55 billion in 2025 and is expected to reach USD 37.70 billion or more by 2035. Usual recycling methods use mechanical processing or chemical breakdown into small, ring-shaped siloxanes. Although these recycled compounds can form new silicone products, the resulting materials are typically lower quality than virgin silicone.The newly detailed process makes recycling silicone waste possible, turning unrecyclable plastic-like materials back into useful industrial ingredients.With a patent already filed, the researchers are turning their attention toward commercial scaling. And are currently hunting for non-toxic phosgene alternatives and designing purification stages to strip out trace contaminants.The study findings were published in the journal Nature on October 28.

title: Humanoid robot achieves 85% task success rate with AGIBOT's GO-3 model
content: Chinese robotics company AGIBOT has unveiled GO-3 Preview, an embodied AI model designed to help robots continuously learn and improve their capabilities. The model uses a World Reasoning Action Model (WRAM) architecture to connect task reasoning, outcome prediction, and action generation. According to AGIBOT, GO-3 Preview has secured first place on three embodied AI benchmarks: RoboDojo, RoboTwin, and RoboColiseum. The company plans to open-source the full model by the end of 2026, allowing wider access to its technology.Enables robot learningGO-3 Preview is a model designed to help robots acquire new skills, adapt to unfamiliar tasks, and improve through real-world experience. The model uses a World Reasoning Action Model (WRAM) architecture that connects reasoning, prediction and physical action, allowing robots to interpret instructions, anticipate outcomes and translate decisions into movements.Launched on October 29, GO-3 Preview is designed to support continuous learning across three stages: pre-training, post-training and deployment. AgiBot says the model has secured first place on three embodied AI leaderboards: RoboDojo, RoboTwin and RoboColiseum. The company plans to release the complete model as open source by the end of 2026.The underlying approach combines two types of training data. First-person human videos provide examples of how people interact with objects and perform everyday activities, while robot trajectories connect visual observations with physical actions and their outcomes. By increasing the model’s learning capacity, AgiBot aims to turn these different sources of experience into transferable skills that robots can apply to tasks they have not encountered before.During pre-training, GO-3 Preview is designed to perform unfamiliar tasks in different environments, including homes, kitchens and multi-robot settings. AgiBot says the model can also handle dexterous manipulation without requiring additional fine-tuning for every new activity.A small number of demonstrations can teach the system complex, multi-step activities. One example involves preparing jianbing, a traditional Chinese savory crepe, which requires a robot to coordinate several delicate movements. The model can also assemble Lego pieces after fine-tuning, with an AI agent coordinating the individual steps.This approach is intended to reduce the amount of task-specific training required when deploying robots in new environments. Instead of building a separate model for every activity, the system can draw on previously acquired knowledge and adapt it to different situations.For post-training, AGIBOT developed Genie Evolver, a distributed training system that combines data from approximately 100 physical robots with physics simulations and world models. The system allows robots to practice tasks, evaluate their performance and improve through repeated attempts.GO-3 improves autonomyIn one demonstration involving tabletop curling, a robot exceeded the average performance of tested humans after four hours of online practice. In another experiment, it successfully removed five consecutive blocks from a block tower without causing it to collapse.These demonstrations highlight how the training framework uses repeated interaction and feedback to improve physical manipulation skills. Combining real-world robot experience with simulation also provides additional opportunities to practice tasks without relying entirely on physical trials.GO-3 Preview also incorporates AGIBOT’s Genie Master agent framework, which connects decision-making, task execution and feedback. The system is designed to let robots identify mistakes during operation, adjust their behavior and retain useful experience for subsequent attempts.AGIBOT demonstrated this capability using a G2 robot deployed in a real convenience store. The robot identified the causes of its own failures, modified its approach and stored the resulting knowledge without requiring human demonstrations or additional manual tuning.Its success rate across the complete task workflow increased from 28.6 percent on the first day to a stable 85.7 percent after five days. On a separate task involving hanging small hooks, the company reported a 17.7-percentage-point improvement in single-task success compared with conventional supervised fine-tuning.Unlike training approaches that largely depend on preparing datasets and updating models before deployment, this framework allows robots to continue learning while performing actual jobs. The combination of large-scale pre-training, distributed post-training and feedback-driven learning after deployment forms the basis of GO-3 Preview. AgiBot’s planned open-source release could give researchers and developers access to the architecture and help expand its use in embodied AI applications.

title: Fast nuclear reactors could use 100 times less uranium for clean power
content:
One way to understand nuclear reactors is to think of them as giant kettles. That’s because they share the same basic principle: both rely on heat to turn water into steam. In nuclear power plants, however, that steam is utilized to generate vast amounts of low-carbon electricity.
This is made possible through a process called nuclear fission, in which a neutron hits the nucleus of a heavy atom, such as uranium, causing it to split and release energy and more neutrons. But there’s a catch. The process also leaves behind a lot of radioactive waste that can remain dangerous for thousands of years.

title: World record-setting micro-LED hits 2.75 GHz, consuming just 25 mW
content: A microscopic LED could offer data centers a more energy-efficient way to move information between computing systems. Researchers from the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign and the University of Notre Dame have developed a micro-LED with record optical switching performance. The device achieves an optical modulation bandwidth of 2.75 gigahertz while consuming just 25 milliwatts of power.The achievement could help reduce the energy demands of short-range optical communications. Data centers increasingly rely on light-based links to move information at high speeds. However, conventional optical transmitters typically use lasers, which consume considerable power and generate heat.The researchers believe their design could provide an efficient alternative for these connections. Their findings also establish a development roadmap for engineering smaller LEDs without sacrificing performance.Finding the ideal sizeThe research team focused on gallium nitride quantum well LEDs, a widely used semiconductor design. They investigated how device dimensions affect switching speed and electrical power consumption. Their experiments covered micro-LED diameters ranging from 100 micrometers down to just 2 micrometers.Surprisingly, the smallest devices did not deliver the best overall performance. Researchers identified 5 micrometers as the optimal diameter for balancing bandwidth and power consumption.The optimized device achieved 2.75 GHz of optical modulation bandwidth. This measurement indicates how quickly an LED can switch its light output in response to electrical signals. Beyond that frequency, the optical signal can lose intensity and become less useful for reliable data transmission.Lead author Abdelghany Abouelnagga said the team challenged the assumption that smaller devices always perform better. Their findings provide a systematic approach to evaluating the relationship between device size, switching speed, and energy requirements.Achieving these results also required detailed semiconductor modeling. Researchers examined material imperfections and electrical characteristics that can introduce parasitic effects. These unwanted effects can limit switching performance and reduce efficiency.The team used those models to guide fabrication and optimize the final device. Its results represent a record for optical modulation bandwidth among quantum well LEDs.Challenging data center lasersOptical communication has become increasingly important as data centers handle growing volumes of information. Light-based connections can transmit data at high frequencies with relatively little signal loss. Copper interconnects face greater limitations as transmission speeds increase.Lasers currently dominate many high-speed optical connections. However, their power requirements create additional challenges for facilities already managing substantial electricity consumption. Heat generated by optical components also adds to cooling demands.Abouelnagga noted that approximately 90% of data center communications involve distances shorter than 10 meters. These connections could benefit from lower-power optical transmitters.The new micro-LED consumes just 25 milliwatts while responding to electrical signals at gigahertz frequencies. Its small footprint could also support dense arrangements of optical emitters.Researchers envision placing multiple micro-LEDs into two-dimensional arrays. Each emitter could carry an independent stream of information, potentially increasing communication capacity within compact hardware.The study appeared in IEEE Electron Device Letters. Researchers from Illinois and Notre Dame collaborated on the project through their respective engineering departments.Although the technology still requires further development, its performance offers a promising direction for short-range optical links. More efficient micro-LED transmitters could eventually help data centers increase communication speeds without relying exclusively on power-hungry lasers.

title: World’s first legged robot built for explosive atmospheres enters delivery phase
content: The world’s first legged inspection robot for explosive atmospheres is now set to be delivered to its customers. Called ANYmal X, the robot uses an advanced industrial AI stack to execute routine autonomous inspections in hazardous environments.Developed by ANYbotics, the robot is now being shipped to several oil, gas, and chemical industry leaders, including Equinor and DSM-Firmenich.A legged robot could never be made safe for explosive atmospheres“Four years of pioneering engineering with more than ten patents went into ANYmal X,” said Péter Fankhauser, co-founder and CEO of ANYbotics. “Many experts thought a legged robot could never be made safe for explosive atmospheres. Oil, gas and chemical plants are among the most hazardous and most costly places to operate. That makes them the prime case for physical and industrial AI, yet until now the areas that matter most were off-limits to robots like ours. That changes today.”ANYmal X automates high-risk inspection rounds without requiring any facility modifications, navigating complex industrial environments such as steep stairs and narrow walkways. Its integrated thermal, visual, acoustic, and gas sensors detect overheating, leaks, abnormal noise, and equipment wear, logging every reading directly to its corresponding asset. This gives reliability engineers a standardized baseline to track asset health over time, enabling teams to spot early signs of wear and intervene before minor issues escalate into costly plant shutdowns, according to a press release.Comprehensive ignition-risk assessment for ANYmal X robot’s service lifeANYmal X was engineered from the ground up to comply with the oil, gas, and chemical sectors’ strictest safety standards. ANYbotics performed a comprehensive ignition-risk assessment for ANYmal X’s service life and implemented safeguards for each potential ignition source. Each of its components has been designed to minimize ignition risk. ANYmal X’s AI computer and inspection equipment are enclosed in nitrogen-filled, sealed chambers. Non-metallic shells insulate metallic components, conductive feet provide grounding, and automatic cutoffs monitor temperature. All twelve leg actuators and its battery are protected by flameproof casings.“We asked one question over and over: which credible event in the life of a walking robot could create an ignition source, and how do we make sure it never does?” says Andrea Corda, CTO of ANYbotics. “Working closely with the certification bodies, we answered that question component by component. The result is a new explosion-protection approach for an entire class of autonomous mobile robots.”ANYmal X’s onboard software monitors the robot’s condition before, during, and after each mission. It also tests durability against shock, vibration, corrosion, solar radiation, and salt mist to ensure all protective measures function properly in normal use.“A certified robot is only the entry ticket for inspecting oil, gas, and chemicals facilities. ANYmal X is a complete end-to-end inspection solution built for performance, safety, and security. It combines autonomous navigation, industrial AI for data interpretation, and integrations that convert findings directly into maintenance work orders. Today, more than 50 power, metals, and materials customers use this system to run over 120,000 autonomous inspections every month,” added Thierry Obédé, Chief Revenue Officer at ANYbotics.In operation, ANYmal X runs on Shift, ANYbotics’ operations platform for autonomous industrial inspection. Shift schedules robot missions, organizes findings by asset and helps maintenance teams track changes over time. It connects inspection findings with the plant systems teams already use, including SAP, Yokogawa and SLB. To ensure top-tier data protection, the whole system is developed and operated under ISO 27001 standards, as per the release.

title: Two helicopters collide midair near Oregon airport, three lives lost
content: Three people were killed after two helicopters collided midair near an airport in Oregon on Thursday afternoon, October 29, prompting an investigation by federal aviation authorities.The collision involved a Robinson R22 and an Airbus H125 helicopter near McMinnville Municipal Airport, approximately 35 miles southwest of Portland, according to the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA).The Yamhill County Sheriff’s Office said emergency crews responded to reports of the collision at approximately 2:15 p.m. local time. Both helicopters crashed into a private farm field southeast of McMinnville.Authorities confirmed that all three people aboard the aircraft died.The National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) is leading the investigation, with assistance from the FAA. Officials have not established what caused the helicopters to collide.Three people confirmed deadYamhill County Sheriff Sam Elliott identified two of the victims during a Thursday evening news conference.They were 22-year-old Maddie Aasbo, a flight instructor from Texas, and 38-year-old Tyler Delane Sturdevant, a pilot from Newberg, Oregon.The third victim was a student pilot visiting from the United Kingdom. Authorities withheld the person’s identity pending notification of family members.According to the sheriff’s office, Aasbo and the student pilot were aboard the Robinson R22, while Sturdevant was the sole occupant of the Airbus H125.The information differed from an initial FAA statement, which placed one person aboard the Robinson and two aboard the Airbus.The Robinson R22 is a lightweight, two-seat helicopter commonly used for flight training and recreational flying.The Airbus H125, previously known as the AS350, is a larger single-engine helicopter used for various missions, including passenger transportation, aerial work, and emergency services.The aircraft have different sizes and operating capabilities, but investigators have not indicated whether those differences contributed to the collision.One of the helicopters was operated by Jerry Trimble Helicopters, a flight training and helicopter rental company based at McMinnville Municipal Airport.The company confirmed that one of its aircraft was involved in the accident and said it was cooperating with investigators.Federal investigation now underwayEmergency personnel from multiple agencies responded to the crash site, where wreckage from both helicopters was scattered across a rural field.Photographs released by the sheriff’s office showed one helicopter overturned and another severely damaged.The collision also disrupted road traffic in the area.The Oregon Department of Transportation closed Highway 233 approximately one mile west of Dayton, while authorities restricted access to nearby roads to allow emergency crews to work.McMinnville Municipal Airport remained open following the accident, according to reports. The airport serves general aviation traffic and has two paved runways.Investigators from the FAA and NTSB arrived at the scene Thursday evening to examine the wreckage and gather evidence. The investigation will seek to establish the circumstances surrounding the collision, including the aircraft’s movements before impact.However, authorities have not released confirmed information about the helicopters’ flight paths, altitudes, or communications before the crash.No mechanical failure, operational error, or other contributing factor has been identified. The NTSB will determine the probable cause after examining the available evidence.For now, the circumstances that brought the two helicopters into contact near McMinnville Municipal Airport remain unclear.

title: New 100-lbf jet engine reaches test milestone in just four months
content: Beehive Industries has successfully tested a compact jet engine designed to power smaller US military drones and munitions. The 100-pound-force (lbf) Frenzy 6 prototype completed its first engine test in September, advancing the company’s effort to develop affordable propulsion systems for the US military.The test marks an important step toward a potential flight demonstration in 2027. Beehive developed the prototype in just four months after finalizing its requirements with the US Air Force. The company now plans to expand testing before integrating the engine into a flight vehicle.Smaller engine, scalable powerFrenzy 6 belongs to Beehive’s growing family of small jet engines. Its 100-lbf thrust rating places it below the company’s larger 200-lbf Frenzy 8 engine. Both designs target military platforms that need compact propulsion without the cost of conventional aircraft engines.The smaller engine also draws on engineering experience from Frenzy 8. Beehive applied shared design principles and development lessons to accelerate the new prototype. However, Frenzy 6 introduces additional technology intended to keep manufacturing costs competitive.Initial testing took place at Beehive’s Colorado headquarters on September 23. Engineers evaluated the prototype’s ability to start reliably and maintain stable operation. The engine also met the initial performance objectives during the test campaign.Beehive CTO David Kimball said experience with Frenzy 8 helped shorten the development cycle. He also pointed to the larger engine’s performance and high-altitude starting capabilities. The company expects Frenzy 6 to inherit some of those advantages.Additive manufacturing drives developmentA major part of Beehive’s development strategy involves additive manufacturing. The approach allows engineers to produce complex engine components through advanced manufacturing processes. It also offers opportunities to reduce production costs and shorten development timelines.Kimball said the company’s experience with Frenzy 8 helped accelerate Frenzy 6 development. He described the four-month journey from finalized requirements to engine testing as evidence of its manufacturing approach.Beehive secured a $29.7 million US Air Force contract in April. The award supports development of its wider Frenzy engine family. Both engines target military applications where production volume and affordability matter.The company is also preparing its manufacturing infrastructure for larger orders. Its announced expansion plans target annual production capacity exceeding 8,000 jet engines. Investments include additive manufacturing equipment, precision machining capabilities, and additional production facilities.Flight demonstration targeted for 2027Frenzy 6 now enters another round of engine testing. Beehive plans to shift toward vehicle integration once the prototype advances through further evaluations.That work will determine how the engine performs within an operational platform. The company is targeting a flight demonstration in 2027.Beehive Chief Product Officer Gordie Follin said Frenzy 6 packages Frenzy 8’s core capabilities into a smaller design. The engine aims to support smaller munitions and unmanned aircraft that need affordable propulsion.The broader objective involves supplying the US defense sector with engines that manufacturers can produce at scale. Beehive’s planned 8,000-unit annual capacity reflects the production ambitions behind that strategy. Frenzy 6’s upcoming integration work will provide the next indication of how quickly the design can move toward flight.

title: Autonomous cargo plane targets 1,000 miles after two-month build
content: A US aerospace startup backed by Y Combinator has built and flown an autonomous cargo aircraft prototype in under two months, demonstrating its ability to take off, follow a flight route, and land without pilot intervention.Los Angeles-based Aviern is developing unmanned fixed-wing aircraft for regional freight deliveries and military resupply missions. Its long-term goal is to transport 1,000 pounds of cargo over 1,000 miles for less than $1,000 per flight.The company announced the development on October 30, outlining plans to connect America’s roughly 5,000 public-use airports through a network of autonomous cargo aircraft.Unlike conventional cargo planes, Aviern’s aircraft are being designed without cockpits, passenger seats, or onboard crew systems. The company says this approach would free up more space for freight while reducing operating costs.The startup has already demonstrated its autonomous flight technology on a scaled composite aircraft, although its larger cargo-carrying models remain under development.Autonomous flight without pilotsAviern’s prototype can taxi, take off, navigate a predefined route, and land autonomously, according to the company. The startup developed the aircraft’s airframe, autopilot, perception system, and ground-control software in-house.Its autonomy software, called AviernOS, has accumulated more than 150 miles of autonomous flight, according to the company’s website. Aviern says the prototype was designed, built, and flown in less than two months.The development is an early step toward aircraft that could operate without pilots onboard or continuously directing their movements from the ground.The company was founded by Kush Agarwal and Arvin Singh, who have backgrounds in aerospace engineering and aircraft development at the University of California, Los Angeles.Agarwal previously worked on autonomous drones and holds a pilot’s license. Singh has spent years designing and building aircraft, including participating in international aircraft design competitions.The founders argue that existing air freight networks leave thousands of smaller airports largely unused for commercial cargo transportation.Although the US has approximately 5,000 public-use airports, only around 520 are certified for airline service, according to figures cited by Aviern.The company wants to use smaller airports to move urgent shipments, including medical supplies, aircraft components, and other high-value goods, without routing everything through major aviation hubs.Cargo aircraft for remote routesAviern’s website describes an aircraft called the A600, designed to carry 600 pounds of cargo over a range of 600 miles. The proposed aircraft has a maximum takeoff weight of 1,320 pounds and is intended to operate from short or unprepared runways.It would use automotive gasoline or aviation gasoline, with a projected operating cost of approximately $100 per hour. These figures are design specifications rather than independently demonstrated performance. The company is also pursuing a broader objective of carrying 1,000 pounds over 1,000 miles for less than $1,000 per flight.Beyond commercial deliveries, Aviern sees potential applications in military logistics, particularly where sending crewed aircraft or ground convoys would be expensive or dangerous. The startup plans to demonstrate fully autonomous flight using a retrofitted small airplane by the first quarter of 2027.That test would move its autonomy technology from a scaled prototype to a larger aircraft. Aviern then aims to build and fly its purpose-designed cargo aircraft by the first quarter of 2028, followed by commercial operations.However, deploying such aircraft commercially will also depend on regulatory approvals. The company is designing its aircraft around the Federal Aviation Administration’s proposed Part 108 framework for beyond-visual-line-of-sight drone operations.Its longer-term vision extends beyond autonomous aircraft to airports where loading, departures, landings, and turnaround operations require minimal human involvement.For now, Aviern has demonstrated autonomous flight on a scaled prototype. Its planned cargo capacity, range, operating costs, and commercial deployment timeline have yet to be proven.

title: US clears safety hurdle for extended nuclear microreactor testing
content: A US nuclear microreactor has cleared a key safety hurdle ahead of a planned test campaign targeting 60 effective full-power days of operation and at least 150 continuous hours without operator intervention.California-based nuclear technology developer Radiant announced that the US Department of Energy (DOE) has approved the Documented Safety Analysis (DSA) for its Kaleidos microreactor.The approval brings the reactor closer to full-power testing at Idaho National Laboratory (INL), where Radiant plans to evaluate its performance under operating conditions.Unlike preliminary tests that establish whether a reactor can sustain a controlled nuclear chain reaction, the upcoming campaign will examine how Kaleidos performs during extended operation.Radiant says the demonstration will be the industry’s only full-power, extended-duration test of a nuclear microreactor to date.However, the reactor must first pass DOE’s Readiness Review before nuclear operations can begin.Testing beyond criticalityThe planned testing campaign will take place at the National Reactor Innovation Center’s Demonstration of Microreactor Experiments (DOME) facility at INL.The five-phase program will begin with initial criticality, the point at which a reactor achieves a self-sustaining nuclear chain reaction.Testing will then progress through increasingly higher power levels, allowing engineers to evaluate the reactor core, instrumentation, and integrated systems under operating conditions.The campaign targets 60 effective full-power days (EFPD) over several months. This represents the equivalent of 60 days of operation at full power, rather than necessarily 60 consecutive days.Another major objective is to demonstrate at least 150 hours of uninterrupted operation at full power without operator intervention.The test would help establish whether the reactor can maintain sustained operation without requiring constant human adjustments.Radiant’s chief nuclear officer, Rita Baranwal, said the approval covers a broader demonstration than initial criticality alone.“This approval for full power demonstration is a first within the microreactor industry. It moves us forward to test our complete reactor system under sustained operating conditions.”The latest approval follows DOE’s acceptance of Radiant’s preliminary safety analysis in February 2026.Toward commercial deploymentKaleidos is a transportable nuclear microreactor designed to provide electricity for military installations, industrial facilities, and locations requiring reliable power.The reactor has a planned electrical output of 1 megawatt and is designed to be transported by land, sea, or air.Radiant built the unit at its El Segundo, California, facility and shipped it to Idaho National Laboratory in August 2026.The company plans to test a reactor design and custom fuel similar to those intended for commercial customers.This approach is intended to generate operating data directly relevant to future deployments, rather than relying solely on smaller experimental systems.Radiant plans to manufacture Kaleidos units at its R-50 facility in Oak Ridge, Tennessee.The company is targeting its first commercial deliveries to Buckley Space Force Base in Colorado and Fort Benning in Georgia in 2028.Earlier in October, the US Navy also selected Radiant to deploy Kaleidos at Naval Weapons Station Crane in Indiana.These projects reflect growing military interest in compact nuclear reactors that could provide power independently of conventional electricity grids.Before testing begins, DOE’s Readiness Review must determine whether the reactor, supporting systems, and operating personnel are prepared for nuclear operations.If the review is successful, Radiant can proceed with fueling Kaleidos and beginning its planned test campaign.The reactor has not yet demonstrated the full-power endurance or unattended operation targeted in the program.

title: US tests self-powered counter-drone system that can be set up quickly
content: Soldiers in the United States are testing rapidly deployable counter-drone systems. They trained on Trust Automation’s Rapidly Deployable Small-Unmanned Air Defense System, or RD-SUADS, a palletized counter-drone system. RD-SUADS is the air-transportable member of Trust Automation’s Small-Unmanned Air Defense System family, designed to detect, track, identify and defeat small drones at bases and deployed sites. The company built it to be shipped and set up quickly without relying on local power.Counter drone system can fit on standard 463L military cargo palletOne of the most significant features of RD-SUADS is its compact, palletized configuration. The entire system is designed to fit on a standard 463L military cargo pallet, allowing it to be transported aboard military aircraft such as the C-130 Hercules and C-17 Globemaster III.This configuration significantly simplifies transportation and deployment, enabling U.S. forces to move counter-drone capabilities to operational locations without requiring specialised transport arrangements.The system also incorporates an integrated diesel generator, providing up to four days of independent operation between refueling. This allows RD-SUADS to function at remote locations where conventional electrical infrastructure may be unavailable.“Soldiers and Airmen at Grafenwoehr Training Area are assessing how multi-service training can strengthen the response to evolving unmanned aircraft system threats. Train together. Adapt faster. Build readiness,” said the U.S. Army in a post on X.Counter drone system has integrated diesel generatorPromoting combat agility, this C‑sUAS is a self-contained, self-powered system that fits within a 463L pallet, enabling easy transport via military aircraft. Equipped with an integrated diesel generator with standalone operational capacity for four days between refueling. Additionally, the shore power interface allows sites with power infrastructure operate the system utilizing standard DoD generator connections and base power connections.For deployment at permanent military installations, the fixed-site C-sUAS tower can be integrated as a group or for smaller bases be standalone enabling diverse base protection and 360-degree security. The base command located SUADS server manages all base C-sUAS sensors, fuses their data into a common operating picture, and allows various mitigation techniques to be activated for a layered base defense solution.Recently, the U.S. military announced the successful completion of a U.S. Army operational assessment of its Small-Unmanned Air Defense System (SUADS). Trust Automation’s SUADS detected and engaged UAS between approximately two and six kilometers away, with potential coverage extending to approximately seven kilometers under favorable conditions. Defeat effectiveness exceeded approximately 75 to 80 percent, while operator observations indicated the system was even more effective at preventing hostile UAS from successfully completing their missions. Interview participants were also not aware of any enemy UAS that penetrated the defended area as a threat within the identified operational ranges without first being detected by the system.“UAS are increasingly being used to find, track and target forces on the battlefield, making early awareness critical to protecting soldiers and keeping operations moving,” said MAJ Patrick Smith, Battalion Executive Officer. “The system consistently provided layered surveillance, early warning, positive target identification, and electronic defeat of hostile UAS before enemy systems could successfully conduct reconnaissance, target acquisition, or attack missions.”
