title: New Treatment Strategy Makes Cancer Cells Run Out of Energy and Die
content:
Leukemia is a type of cancer that affects the blood and bone marrow, where blood cells are produced. It typically causes the uncontrolled growth of abnormal white blood cells, which crowd out healthy blood cells and interfere with the body’s ability to fight infections, carry oxygen, and prevent bleeding. Credit: Shutterstock
A promising new drug combination exploits a metabolic vulnerability in leukemia cells.
Researchers have discovered a way to kill leukemia cells by forcing them to remain highly active even as their energy supply is disrupted. The experimental treatment has produced promising results in mice and patient-derived cancer cells, including a particularly aggressive form of the disease that often resists treatment.
The approach targets acute myeloid leukemia (AML), a rapidly progressing cancer of the blood and bone marrow that interferes with normal blood cell production. Developed by researchers at the University of Gothenburg in Sweden and Case Western Reserve University in Cleveland, the treatment exploits the energy demands of malignant cells rather than directly attacking their DNA.
Forcing Cancer Cells to Work Without Enough Energy
At the center of the strategy is mTOR, a protein that helps regulate cell growth, metabolism, and activity. Under normal conditions, cells adjust these processes according to their available resources. The researchers designed a molecule called AcTor that blocks a signaling protein involved in controlling mTOR, allowing growth signals to remain active even when cellular energy production is impaired.
AcTor was combined with ixazomib (IXZ), a drug used to inhibit cancer cell proliferation. Together, the treatments disrupt energy production in mitochondria while preventing leukemia cells from slowing their activity. Unable to balance their energy needs with their available resources, the cancer cells experience severe stress and die.
Leif Eriksson, Professor of Physical Chemistry at the University of Gothenburg. Credit: Jesper Larsson
The treatment emerged from a collaboration between biochemist Boaz Tirosh and computational chemist Leif Eriksson, whose expertise helped turn the underlying hypothesis into a potential drug.
“Boaz Tirosh is a biochemist and understands the processes taking place within a cell. It was he who put forward the hypothesis for this treatment. I am a computational chemist and have designed a molecule that enters the cancerous cell and alters it in the way we want,” says Leif Eriksson, Professor of Physical Chemistry at the University of Gothenburg.
Experimental Treatment Targets Aggressive Leukemia
In a study published in
Molecular Cancer
, the combination of AcTor and ixazomib demonstrated strong activity against AML in laboratory cell lines, primary samples from patients, and animal experiments. It also remained effective against TP53-mutant AML, an especially aggressive form of leukemia associated with poor outcomes and limited treatment options.
The researchers found that the treatment eliminated malignant blood cells as well as leukemic stem cells. These stem cells can survive conventional therapies and regenerate the disease, contributing to relapse. The mouse experiments also suggested that the treatment could avoid the development of drug resistance, although this has not been established in patients.
Boaz Tirosh, Professor of Biochemistry at the Case Western Reserve University in Cleveland. Credit: Matt Schiffler
“It’s a completely new method and does not affect healthy blood cells; furthermore, our studies in mice show that drug resistance is avoided, which can otherwise happen,” says Leif Eriksson.
A Potential Biomarker for Monitoring Treatment
The researchers also detected a biological response that might eventually help doctors assess whether the treatment is working. Cells exposed to the drug combination released a protein called ADM2, which could potentially serve as a measurable indicator of treatment activity.
“We also observed that our treatment triggered the release of a protein (ADM2), which could therefore serve as a biomarker for the treatment’s response. This could guide future translational and clinical studies,” says Leif Eriksson.
The findings remain preclinical, meaning that the combination has not yet been shown to be safe or effective in humans. Further studies will be needed to confirm its activity, evaluate potential side effects, and determine whether it can progress to clinical trials. Patients with relapsed or refractory AML, whose disease has returned or failed to respond to treatment, could be among those who might benefit if the approach eventually proves successful.
Shifting Cancer Research Toward Metabolism
Instead of relying primarily on treatments that damage cancer cell DNA, the research focuses on disrupting the metabolic processes that allow leukemia cells to survive.
“Our study is an example of the shift toward focusing research on cancer metabolism within cells, rather than relying solely on methods that damage DNA. Drug development is very expensive, but we hope that our findings will generate sufficient interest to enable us to continue our research into a cure for this serious disease,” says Leif Eriksson.

title: A Promising Way To Reverse Cognitive Decline Just Failed a Major Clinical Test
content:
A treatment that can reduce stroke risk may not offer the same benefits for cognition. New research reveals an important distinction between preventing strokes and improving brain function. Credit: Shutterstock
Restoring blood flow to the brain seemed a promising way to protect thinking skills, but opening severely narrowed arteries did not deliver the cognitive boost researchers hoped for.
Columbia
-led randomized trial found that people with severe carotid artery narrowing gained no additional cognitive benefit from stenting or surgery compared with medication alone over one year. The findings challenge the idea that reopening these arteries can reverse cognitive decline in patients without associated symptoms.
“We had hoped that improving blood flow in the brain in this way would improve cognition—and there were tantalizing clues from animal studies and case series that it would,” says study leader Randolph Marshall, MD, the Elisabeth K. Harris Professor of Neurology at Columbia University Vagelos College of Physicians and Surgeons. “But when we put it to the test in a randomized clinical trial, comparing cognition after opening the blockage or treatment with medication alone, we did not see a difference.”
Why Opening Carotid Arteries Seemed Promising
The carotid arteries run through the neck and supply blood to the brain. Severe narrowing, known as carotid stenosis, is associated with cognitive impairment even in people who have never had a stroke. The link is particularly apparent when blood flow to the brain is reduced.
That connection raised a compelling possibility: restoring circulation might help preserve or improve cognition. Stenting holds a narrowed artery open, while surgery removes the material causing the blockage.
“We’ve thought for a long time that improving cognition by restoring blood flow with stenting or surgery could improve cognition, but until our study, the hypothesis had never been tested in a randomized clinical trial.”
To investigate, the researchers enrolled 291 patients in CREST-H, all with carotid artery narrowing of at least 70% but no associated symptoms. They assessed brain blood flow and cognition at enrollment and again one year later. Cognitive scores improved slightly in both groups, but patients who underwent a procedure did no better than those treated with medication alone.
Stroke Prevention Showed a Different Result
CREST-H was part of CREST-2, a larger multicenter trial that Marshall helped design to compare approaches to preventing strokes in people with severe carotid blockages. In that trial, adding stenting to medication cut strokes by about half compared with medication alone. Surgery to remove the blockage did not show the same benefit.
“Those results do appear to have changed practice already, and more of these patients are getting stents,” says Marshall. The cognitive findings, however, suggest that patients should not expect the procedure to improve their thinking skills beyond what medication alone provides.
“We concluded that revascularization to reverse cognitive decline in these patients cannot be expected. Therefore, we need to reinforce the importance of preventing carotid stenosis to avoid its consequences,” says Marshall.

title: Scientists Challenge a Long-Held Belief About Artificial Sweeteners
content:
Sugar substitutes offer a way to enjoy sweet foods and drinks while reducing added sugar and calories. Although concerns remain about their effects on appetite, metabolism, and long-term health, recent research suggests they may support weight management without increasing cravings for sweetness. Credit: Stock
New evidence challenges the idea that consuming more sweetness increases cravings or appetite.
Replacing sugar with artificial sweeteners does not appear to increase hunger, intensify cravings for sweet foods, or interfere with weight management, according to a review of three major European clinical trials. The research also found little evidence that consuming a sweeter diet harms metabolic health, challenging concerns that sweetness itself encourages overeating.
The findings come from the SWEET, SWITCH, and Sweet Tooth research programs, which examined how sugar substitutes and overall dietary sweetness affect body weight, appetite, food preferences, and metabolic health.
Sugar Substitutes and Weight Loss
In a yearlong weight maintenance trial, participants in the SWEET consortium who consumed non-nutritive sweeteners maintained slightly greater weight loss than those who avoided them. The difference was largest among participants who consistently followed their assigned diets.
The 52-week SWITCH trial produced similar results. Participants who drank beverages containing non-nutritive sweeteners lost somewhat more weight than those who drank water, although the difference was not considered clinically meaningful.
The Sweet Tooth trial instead examined whether increasing or decreasing dietary sweetness affected body weight without a weight loss intervention. Neither approach produced meaningful changes in weight or body composition.
Do Artificial Sweeteners Increase Cravings?
Researchers also investigated whether regular exposure to sweetness encourages people to seek more sugary foods or consume additional calories. Across the trials, sweeteners did not consistently increase hunger, cravings, or overall food intake.
In the SWEET trial, participants who avoided sweeteners developed a stronger preference for sweet foods over time, while those consuming them did not. Changing the overall sweetness of participants’ diets also had little measurable effect on appetite or taste preferences.
Professor Graham Finlayson of the University of Leeds explained: “A common concern is that replacing sugar with non-nutritive sweeteners might lead to a stronger preference for sugary sweet foods or stimulate appetite. Across these controlled studies, that prediction was not supported. Sweeteners are not a weight-management strategy by themselves, but they can provide a useful way to reduce sugar while retaining sweetness within a broader healthy diet.”
Effects on Blood Sugar and Heart Health
The trials also measured blood glucose, insulin, cholesterol, blood pressure, liver enzymes, and other indicators of metabolic and cardiovascular health. Most remained comparable between participants consuming sweeteners and those avoiding them.
Some short-term experiments found that replacing sugar with sweeteners reduced post-meal increases in blood glucose and insulin. One substudy also identified modest changes in gut bacteria, but these were not accompanied by worsening cardiometabolic risk markers.
Why Health Recommendations Differ
Health organizations have issued conflicting guidance about non-nutritive sweeteners. The World Health Organization has cautioned against relying on them for long-term weight control, while several professional organizations in the United Kingdom consider them useful for reducing sugar intake.
Much of the disagreement comes from differences between observational studies and randomized controlled trials. Observational research sometimes links sweetener consumption to metabolic health risks, but people already at higher risk may be more likely to use sugar substitutes. Randomized trials, which can better isolate cause and effect, generally report neutral or favorable outcomes when sweeteners replace sugar.
Important Questions Remain
Most participants were adults with overweight, often enrolled in structured dietary programs. The findings may not apply equally to children, adolescents, or people following different eating patterns. Some studies also experienced participant dropout and relied on self-reported dietary information.
The results suggest that replacing sugar with non-nutritive sweeteners can support weight management without detectable adverse effects on appetite or metabolic health during the periods studied. However, the trials cannot rule out effects under other conditions, and the consequences of long-term consumption remain uncertain.

title: These Tiny Magnetic Waves Could Unlock a New Era of Ultra-Efficient Computers
content:
A study has revealed that magnons are surprisingly long-lived – an important insight for designing spintronic materials in the future. In the image, an ultrashort laser pulse triggers collective excitations in an antiferromagnetic material, forming a wave. A new X-ray technique at SwissFEL allowed researchers to follow how these collective excitations, such as magnons, evolve. Credit: Paul Scherrer Institute PSI/Hiroki Ueda
Scientists have discovered that tiny magnetic excitations can persist much longer than expected.
Magnetic waves inside a quantum material can hold onto their energy far longer than scientists expected, potentially opening a path toward faster computers that consume less electricity. Researchers at the
Paul Scherrer Institute (PSI)
discovered that these microscopic excitations survive for an unusually long time before transferring their energy to the surrounding crystal structure. That delay could provide enough time to perform the logical operations needed for future computing technologies.
Using advanced X-ray techniques, the team tracked how energy moves among electrons, magnetic excitations, and vibrating atoms across extremely short timescales. “We have now investigated the dynamics of these excitations and, in doing so, have been able to reveal in unprecedented detail all important aspects that happen in the material with a microscopic view,” says Hiroki Ueda, who led the project at PSI. “We are particularly interested in the interrelationship between the various excitations in the material,” explains Ueda.
Computing With Spin Waves Instead of Moving Electrons
Conventional computer chips rely on moving electrical charges through silicon, a process that generates heat and consumes energy. As transistors become increasingly difficult to shrink and demand for computing power continues to grow, researchers are investigating alternative ways to process information. One promising approach is spintronics, a field whose name combines “spin” and “electronics.” Instead of depending entirely on the movement of electrons, spintronic devices could transmit information by manipulating their magnetic properties.
Electrons possess a quantum property called spin, which makes them behave somewhat like tiny magnetic compass needles. When neighboring spins move collectively, they can produce waves called magnons. These waves can carry information through a material without requiring electrons themselves to travel along the same path. The process resembles a stadium wave, where a pattern moves through the crowd even though individual spectators remain in their seats.
Another type of excitation, known as a phonon, represents vibrations of atoms within a crystal lattice. Magnons and phonons are both classified as “quasiparticles” because they behave like entities with measurable energy and momentum without being individual physical particles (such as atoms, electrons, or photons). Understanding how these two types of excitation exchange energy is essential for determining whether spin waves can be controlled efficiently in electronic devices.
Following Magnetic Excitations Across Tiny Fractions of a Second
To investigate these interactions, the researchers studied copper oxide, a magnetic material in which atomic vibrations and magnetism strongly influence one another. “We chose copper oxide because it is a well-known magnetic material with strong interactions between magnetism and the lattice,” said publication first-author Arnau Romaguera of the PSI Center for Photon Science.
The experiment began with an intense, ultrashort laser pulse that excited electrons in the material and triggered coordinated changes in their spins. Magnons emerged within femtoseconds (one quadrillionth of a second). Over the following picoseconds (one-trillionth of a second), the magnons scattered off one another, producing a disordered mixture of magnetic waves.
The transfer of energy from magnons to the vibrating crystal lattice occurred much later, on the scale of nanoseconds (one-billionth of a second). During this process, magnetic excitation energy was converted into phonons. Although a nanosecond is extraordinarily brief in everyday terms, it is a relatively long lifetime for excitations produced by processes occurring on femtosecond timescales.
Why the Magnetic Waves Survive So Long
“Considering the strong coupling between magnetism and the lattice of copper oxide, we were surprised how long it then takes the generated magnons to pass their energy to the lattice,” says Romaguera. Despite the strong connection between the material’s magnetic and atomic properties, the magnons retained their energy much longer than anticipated.
The explanation involves differences in how the two kinds of excitations carry energy and momentum. “The magnons and phonons exhibit very different relationships between their momentum and energy values,” explains Ueda. These differences restrict how efficiently energy can pass from magnetic waves into atomic vibrations.
“This modulates the efficiency in which magnons can transfer their energy to the lattice, leading to the long lifetime of the magnons and providing us with important insights into how to use specifically designed materials to adjust the lifetime of the magnons as desired.”
Advanced X-Rays Reveal the Quantum Energy Flow
Capturing the full sequence required observing different microscopic processes across timescales separated by six orders of magnitude. Earlier experimental approaches could measure individual aspects of spin wave behavior, but they could not provide a unified view of how electronic, magnetic, and lattice excitations interact.
“We used several X-ray techniques for this,” says Romaguera. “What they all have in common is that a highly brilliant X-ray pulse from a free-electron laser is directed at the sample shortly after the optical laser pulse that generates the magnons.”
This approach, known as the pump-probe technique, allows scientists to reconstruct the evolution of a material by changing the delay between the initial optical laser pulse and the X-ray pulse used to examine its response. The team combined two established X-ray methods with a novel application of “time-resolved resonant diffuse scattering.” Experiments took place at the Furka experimental station of SwissFEL (FEL for “free-electron laser”) at PSI, with additional measurements performed at the ESRF synchrotron in Grenoble, France.
Bringing Spintronic Computing Closer to Reality
The researchers also used quantum kinetic simulations to model the transfer of energy among the different excitations. Comparing these calculations with the experimental measurements helped establish whether existing theoretical descriptions could reproduce the observed behavior.
“Our measurements are largely consistent with the theoretical calculations,” explains Ueda. The agreement supports the underlying physical models, although they will need to be adapted to account for the structures and properties of different materials.

title: Astronauts Just Installed a Powerful New Solar Array High Above Earth
content:
NASA astronaut Anil Menon rides the Canadarm2 robotic arm to begin the installation of a roll-out solar array on the International Space Station’s port-side truss structure while orbiting 260 miles above Earth. Credit: NASA+
NASA astronauts have completed another major step in upgrading the International Space Station’s power supply. During a spacewalk lasting more than seven hours, two crew members installed a new solar array that will help generate electricity for the orbiting laboratory, supporting everything from scientific experiments to the station’s eventual retirement.
NASA astronaut Anil Menon and CSA (Canadian Space Agency) astronaut Joshua Kutryk finished their spacewalk outside the International Space Station at 3:08 p.m. EDT on October 29. The mission lasted 7 hours and 11 minutes and brought NASA closer to completing a significant expansion of the station’s electrical power system.
Their primary assignment was to install and deploy an International Space Station Roll-Out Solar Array (IROSA) on the station’s 2A electrical power channel. This channel is part of the network that distributes electricity throughout the massive spacecraft, ensuring that its equipment and systems receive the energy they need.
The newly installed equipment is the seventh of eight roll-out solar arrays planned for the station. Together, these additions will substantially increase the electricity available to support daily operations, research activities, and the station’s eventual safe and controlled return to Earth.
This mosaic depicts the International Space Station pictured from the SpaceX Crew Dragon Endeavour during a fly around of the orbiting lab that took place following its undocking from the Harmony module’s space-facing port on November 8, 2021. Credit: NASA
How the Space Station’s New Solar Arrays Work
The International Space Station relies on sunlight as its primary source of electricity. Its large solar arrays contain thousands of solar cells that convert sunlight directly into electrical energy, much like solar panels installed on homes and buildings.
That electricity powers essential systems, including life support equipment, communications, temperature regulation, and the scientific instruments used by astronauts. When the station travels into Earth’s shadow and can no longer collect sunlight, rechargeable batteries supply stored electricity to keep everything running.
The newer roll-out solar arrays use a different design from the station’s original solar panels. Rather than requiring a large, rigid structure, the new arrays are lightweight and compact enough to be launched in a rolled configuration. Once positioned outside the station, they gradually unfurl, similar to a yoga mat being unrolled.
Although these newer arrays are roughly half the size of the original solar wings, advances in solar cell technology allow them to generate substantial additional electricity. They supplement the station’s older panels, which have gradually lost some of their generating capability after decades of exposure to the harsh environment of space.
The International Space Station is pictured from the SpaceX Crew Dragon Endeavour during a fly around of the orbiting lab that took place following its undocking from the Harmony module’s space-facing port on November 8, 2021. Credit: NASA
NASA Nears Completion of a 30% Power Upgrade
The latest installation leaves just one solar array remaining. During their spacewalk, Menon and Kutryk also performed preliminary work to help prepare for the next installation, reducing the amount of preparation needed during the upcoming mission.
That final spacewalk is scheduled for Thursday, November 5, when the astronauts are expected to install the eighth IROSA on the station’s 3B power channel. NASA will begin live coverage at 6:45 a.m., with the broadcast available through
NASA’s live streaming service
Once all eight arrays are installed, the station’s solar power expansion will be complete. NASA estimates that the upgrades will increase available power by up to 30%, raising the station’s electricity generation capacity from 160 kilowatts to approximately 215 kilowatts.
The additional energy will provide greater electrical capacity for the station’s demanding operations. It will also help ensure that the aging laboratory can continue supporting scientific research and other essential activities during its remaining years in orbit.
Why the Power Upgrade Matters for the Station’s Final Years
The International Space Station has supported continuous human occupation for more than 25 years, serving as a unique research laboratory where scientists can study everything from human health to materials and fluid behavior in microgravity.
Microgravity is the condition of apparent weightlessness experienced by astronauts in orbit. It allows researchers to investigate how physical and biological processes behave when the familiar effects of gravity are greatly reduced. Many of these experiments help scientists prepare for longer missions to the Moon, Mars, and beyond.
Keeping the station operational requires a reliable supply of electricity, especially as its equipment ages and NASA prepares for the end of its service life.
NASA currently plans to retire the International Space Station around 2030. Rather than allowing the enormous structure to fall back to Earth in an uncontrolled manner, the agency intends to guide it through a carefully planned descent, directing surviving debris toward a remote ocean region away from populated areas.
This process is known as a controlled deorbit. The new solar arrays will help provide electricity for the station’s critical systems as it continues operating and prepares for that eventual final mission.
The latest excursion, designated U.S. spacewalk 100, also marked an important personal milestone for the two astronauts. It was Menon’s fourth spacewalk and Kutryk’s first.
Overall, it was the 285th spacewalk conducted in support of the International Space Station’s construction, maintenance, and upgrades, highlighting the extensive work required to keep one of humanity’s most ambitious engineering projects operating in orbit.

title: Did Venus Eat Its Own Moon? Scientists Uncover a Shocking Possibility
content:
Image of Earth’s fiery twin, Venus. Credit: NASA/JPL/Caltech
Venus may have swallowed its own moon, according to computer simulations that point to the planet’s slow spin as the culprit.
Venus is Earth’s near-twin in size, mass, and structure, but it has no moon. Scientists have long wondered whether the planet never experienced a moon-forming collision or whether a massive object smashed apart a moon it once had.
“My study shows Venus didn’t require a catastrophe to arrive at what we can see today,” said Stephen Kane, an astrophysicist at the University of California, Riverside, and lead author of the new research. “It turns out the gravity of the planet itself combined with the rate at which it spins naturally caused the moon to collapse on top of it.”
The study, published in
The Astrophysical Journal
, does not establish that Venus ever had a moon, although Kane believes it may have. His models explore what would have happened to a hypothetical companion.
Slow rotation can draw moons inward
The relationship between a planet’s spin and its moon’s orbit is measurable here on Earth. Mirrors left on the moon by NASA’s Apollo 11 mission allow scientists to precisely track its distance from our planet. “We know that the moon is slowly moving away from the planet, at a rate of around four centimeters per year,” Kane said. That is about 1.6 inches annually.
Earth completes a rotation every 24 hours, and energy transferred from that relatively fast spin to the moon moves it farther away. Venus takes 243 Earth days to turn once. Its slow rotation gives a moon a different fate, with gravity drawing it inward instead.
Kane tested that process with computer models based on the physics of gravitational interactions between planetary bodies. He first reproduced the evolution of Earth and its moon to check that the model accurately represented a known system. Then he varied Venus’ rotation rate and the masses of its hypothetical moons, testing companions from half to ten times the mass of Earth’s moon.
“When I made this discovery, I was shocked,” Kane said. “I thought surely the broad range of scenarios I was exploring would lead to a variety of results. But it all went pretty much in the same direction.”
In most simulations, the moon crashed into Venus. More massive moons collided with the planet sooner. The results suggest that even if Venus had formed a moon, it could not have kept it indefinitely.
Does life need a large moon?
“When people think about Earth twins around other stars, one question they ask is, ‘Does it have a moon?’” Kane said. “My study shows a disturbing scenario for many of those cases. If these planets don’t rotate fast enough, the moon will crash to the surface, and that would change the course of history for those planets.”
Scientists searching for potentially habitable worlds often focus on planets resembling Earth, with moons among the factors they consider. Earth’s moon drives tides and may have helped keep the planet geologically active. Whether those contributions make a large moon necessary for life remains unknown.
“My feeling is there are benefits to having a moon, but it isn’t required for habitability,” Kane said. “The moon has definitely changed the way Earth has evolved through time, but we don’t fully know how important that role is.”
A moon crashing into Venus would have transferred enormous amounts of energy and angular momentum, a measure of rotational motion, to the planet. That could have changed its rotation, geology, and climate, with consequences for another unresolved question about Earth’s nearest planetary neighbor. If Venus once had oceans or other conditions favorable to life, such an impact could have altered the course of its evolution.
Finding physical evidence of a collision would be difficult. Roughly 80% of Venus’ surface is similar in age, evidence of a major resurfacing event about a billion years ago that erased much of the planet’s earlier geological history.
Scientists may have better prospects beneath the surface. Earth’s moon is thought to have formed after a massive collision early in our planet’s history, and seismic studies have revealed unusual structures deep inside Earth that may be remnants of that event. Similar measurements on Venus could offer clues about whether it once absorbed a moon.
Reference: “Tidal Demise: The Evolution and Fate of a Hypothetical Venus Moon” by Stephen R. Kane, Franck Selsis, Jérémy Leconte and Sean N. Raymond, 14 September 2026,
The Astrophysical Journal

title: New Microscope Technology Captures the Hidden World Inside Living Cells Like Never Before
content:
Mitochondrial outer membrane imaged with SPIFFI (left) versus widefield microscopy (right). Credit: EPFL LBEN CC BY SA
A new imaging technique allows scientists to capture fleeting cellular processes that conventional microscopes struggle to resolve.
Living cells are constantly in motion, but capturing their smallest structures in sharp detail has long been a challenge. Traditional super-resolution microscopy often requires hundreds or thousands of images to reveal features too small for conventional light microscopes. When structures move during that process, the resulting images can become blurred. Now, researchers have developed a technique that captures these microscopic details in a single camera exposure.
The new method, called Spatial Polarization-Induced Fluorescence Fluctuation Imaging (SPIFFI), was developed by a team led by Aleksandra Radenovic at the Laboratory of Nanoscale Biology (LBEN) in EPFL’s School of Engineering. Published in
Nature Methods
, the research demonstrates up to a twofold improvement in image resolution, allowing scientists to distinguish structures as small as 160 to 170 nanometers while observing living cells.
Why Moving Cells Are So Difficult to Image
Super-resolution microscopy has transformed cell biology by revealing structures that conventional light microscopes cannot clearly distinguish. Many established techniques rely on fluorescent molecules that emit light when illuminated by a laser. Scientists analyze subtle changes in this fluorescence across large sequences of images, then combine the information to reconstruct a sharper picture.
These approaches work particularly well with chemically preserved cells, where structures remain stationary during imaging. Living cells present a different challenge. Mitochondria continually change shape, microtubules reorganize, and DNA moves within the cell. Capturing multiple frames takes time, allowing these structures to shift before the final image can be assembled.
Video demonstrating the ability of SPIFFI to capture rapid cellular dynamics and extract molecular orientation at the same time. Credit: EPFL LBEN CC BY SA 4.0
“Essentially, previous approaches used temporal information to resolve spatial resolution, but this doesn’t work very well on living cells,” explains first author and LBEN PhD student Wei Guo.
Using Polarized Light to Reveal Hidden Structures
Instead of collecting information over many exposures, SPIFFI takes advantage of a property of fluorescent light known as polarization. Fluorescent molecules emit light whose waves tend to oscillate in particular directions, depending on the molecules’ orientation. These directional differences contain spatial information that conventional fluorescence imaging does not fully exploit.
SPIFFI separates the emitted light into four channels, each sensitive to a different polarization component. By comparing the four images captured during the same exposure, the system can recover fine structural details without needing to accumulate information across hundreds of frames.
The researchers demonstrated the technique by imaging moving mitochondria and microtubules, as well as cellular structures undergoing fusion and splitting. These rapid changes are difficult to resolve with methods that require multiple exposures to produce one super-resolution image.
“Our experiments show that SPIFFI can capture fast-moving processes within cells, while enabling high-throughput, multi-dimensional imaging beyond the limits of conventional microscopes,” Radenovic summarizes.
Turning Super-Resolution Images Into Videos
Because SPIFFI produces a super-resolved image from every camera exposure, successive frames can be combined to create videos of cellular activity without sacrificing spatial resolution through multi-frame reconstruction.
“With previous techniques, taking many images would only result in one super-resolved frame. With SPIFFI, every frame is super-resolved, meaning we can now produce super-resolution videos of live cells,” Guo says. “We also seamlessly integrated SPIFFI images with existing fluctuation-based methods for post-processing, achieving resolutions of about 80 nanometers.”
The team is now working to make the imaging system more compact and integrate it with three-dimensional microscopy. Because SPIFFI’s optical components can be incorporated into existing fluorescence microscopes, the technique could eventually support research in cell biology, neuroscience, biophysics, and drug discovery, particularly when scientists need to observe rapid structural changes inside living cells.
Reference: “SPIFFI enables single-shot super-resolution and multidimensional imaging” by Wei Guo (郭威), Lely Feletti and Aleksandra Radenovic, 31 August 2026,
Nature Methods
DOI: 10.1038/s41592-026-03196-6

title: 60,000-Year-Old Discovery in South Africa Reveals a Surprising Clue About Early Humans
content:
A photo of the Kilpdrift Complex located within the coastal cliffs in the De Hoop Nature Reserve in South Africa where the samples for the study were collected. Credit: Ole F. Unhammer/Universitetet i Bergen
Where ancient DNA rarely survives, antelope protein preserved with ochre pigment offers clues to the technical skills and possible symbolic practices of early humans.
A 60,000-year-old ochre-rich surface in South Africa still holds traces of an antelope protein, preserving a clue to how early humans used the mineral pigment. Ochre is a naturally occurring, iron-rich material that can be ground into a colored powder. Researchers identified type I collagen, a structural protein found in animal tissues, from the common eland,
Taurotragus oryx
. The finding provides molecular evidence that animal-derived materials were associated with ochre use during the Middle Stone Age.
The protein could reflect two different activities. People may have deliberately mixed animal-derived materials into the ochre, or eland hides treated with the pigment may have been present at the site. Evidence of organic components mixed with ochre has been extremely rare, particularly in Africa, so recovering these traces offers a way to investigate materials that are no longer visible in the archaeological record.
Matching ancient proteins to an antelope
The surface was found at the Kilpdrift Complex, a Middle and Later Stone Age archaeological site within the coastal cliffs of South Africa’s De Hoop Nature Reserve. A team from Kyushu University, Universitetet i Bergen, and the University of Copenhagen examined archived sediment samples from the site to search for preserved proteins. Their findings are published in
Proceedings of the Royal Society B
An eland is a large plains antelope found in East and Southern Africa. Credit: Takumi Tsutaya/Kyushu University
To detect those traces, the researchers turned to paleoproteomics, the large-scale analysis of ancient proteins. This growing field in archaeology and paleontology examines proteins preserved in materials collected at archaeological sites. Here, it allowed the team to look for biological evidence within the ochre-rich sediments.
The researchers extracted proteins from the samples and analyzed them using liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry, or LC-MS/MS. They then compared the resulting protein fragments with entries in large protein databases and a custom collagen reference database to identify the animal they came from. Those comparisons identified collagen from the common eland.
First author Zahra Haghighi pictured preparing a sample in a clean laboratory for palaeoprotemic analysis. Credit: Takumi Tsutaya/Kyushu University
Reconstructing Stone Age life through proteins
The association between eland materials and ochre adds evidence of the complex technical behaviors of early
Homo sapiens
, with possible symbolic roles as well. Although the traces do not establish exactly how the materials were used, they open another route to studying the place of pigments and animal-derived materials in early human daily life.
The successful recovery also demonstrates that ancient proteins can be identified in archaeological sediments even in challenging African environments where ancient DNA rarely survives. Paleoproteomics could therefore help archaeologists investigate biological materials whose visible remains have disappeared.
Reference: “Palaeoproteomic investigation of archaeological sediments associated with ochre use in the Middle Stone Age of southern Africa” by Zahra Haghighi, Takumi Tsutaya, Elizabeth C. Velliky, Simon Armitage, Christopher Miller, Meaghan Mackie, Francesco d’Errico, Gaudry Troche, Jesper Olsen, Karen van Niekerk, Christopher Henshilwood and Enrico Cappellini, 1 October 2026,

title: 237-Million-Year-Old Fossils Reveal an Amphibian That Shouldn’t Have Existed
content:
An illustrated rendering of Gerrothoroax maritumus, informed by newly discovered fossil evidence of the creature, which is the first fully marine amphibian on record. AI was sparingly used in the rendering’s creation to adjust lighting, brightness, fish skin, and amphibian skin. Credit: Chen Geng/Guizhou University
Two fossils from China point to the first known fully marine amphibian, revealing an ancient exception to the freshwater dependence of its living relatives.
An armored amphibian nearly three feet long appears to have lived on the seafloor hundreds of miles from a large landmass. How did it survive in salt water when no known amphibian alive today can live entirely at sea?
Two nearly complete skeletons from China offer clues. Researchers from the University of California, Davis, Peking University, and the Geological Museum of Guizhou identified the animal as
Gerrothorax maritimus
, which lived nearly 237 million years ago during the Late Triassic. Their study, published in
Nature Ecology & Evolution
, reports the first fossil evidence of a fully marine amphibian.
Preserved fingers point to ocean life
The skeletons were discovered in China’s Guizhou Province, in an area once covered by ocean. Researchers have been reconstructing the ecosystem preserved there through its fossils.
“This area is part of an ecosystem that we’ve been looking at and trying to reconstruct,” said study corresponding author Ryosuke Motani, a professor in the
Department of Earth and P
anetary Sciences
at UC Davis. “We’ve been mostly studying marine reptiles and the fish from this place, but now we also have this amphibian, and it’s a sort of very unusual member of the lineage.”
New fossil evidence reveals the first fully marine amphibian, Gerrothorax maritimus, which dates to the Late Triassic period nearly 237 million years ago. The animal had a flattened body that was covered in bony armor, a potential defense mechanism against predators like ichthyosaurs. Credit: Ryosuke Motani, UC Davis
Finding the skeletons in deep-sea sediments helped establish their marine setting. Their remarkable completeness also supported the researchers’ interpretation that the animals had lived there.
“Carcasses at sea, unless they sink to the bottom right away, tend to dry out and lose limbs prior to sinking to the bottom,” said Motani. “But these animals had their fingers preserved, so that means they probably died near where they lived.”
Geochemical analyses provided further evidence. The proportions of strontium isotopes, forms of the same element with different atomic masses, closely resembled those expected in Late Triassic seawater.
Professor Ryosuke Motani sits in his office at UC Davis. Credit: Greg Watry/UC Davis
Could armor solve the salt problem?
The well-preserved skeletons also revealed an animal with a flattened, disc-shaped body covered in bony armor. That covering may have protected it against predators such as ichthyosaurs, a group of marine reptiles.
“If you think about today’s amphibians, this animal is unusual because it’s big,” Motani said. “It’s probably, body mass-wise, about the same as the giant salamander, but what’s different is that giant salamanders are elongated whereas this animal is really chunky.”
The armor could also help explain how
G. maritimus
managed life in the ocean. Mammals, reptiles, and birds include species that can obtain the food and water they need at sea. Modern amphibians, however, have skin poorly suited to salt water.
“That skin is permeable, and that allows the animals to use it for multiple purposes,” said Motani. “They use it for respiration and water intake, so amphibians don’t drink or breathe through the mouth because they can do both through the skin.”
The fossilized left hand of the newly discovered prehistoric marine amphibian Gerrothorax maritimus. Credit: Ryosuke Motani/UC Davis
This dependence on permeable skin ties modern amphibians to freshwater environments. Fewer than 2% of the more than 8,000 living species show any degree of salt tolerance. Even the crab-eating frog, which can tolerate some salt, loses weight in brackish water and needs to recover in fresh water. Being able to endure those conditions does not amount to independence from fresh water.
The researchers propose that
G. maritimus
overcame this limitation through its armor and more fish-like biology. Under their explanation, the bony covering would have prevented water absorption through the skin. The animal would therefore have needed to drink salt water through its mouth and absorb water through its digestive tract. Gills, which are present in the genus
Gerrothorax
, could have filtered out the salt.
The trunk or central part of fossilized Gerrothorax maritimus, a marine amphibian. Credit: Ryosuke Motani/UC Davis
Clues to a seafloor ambush hunter
Its armor and skull shape also offered clues to how it fed. The researchers hypothesize that
G. maritimus
lived on the bottom and captured prey by suction, a feeding style Motani compared with that of the wobbegong, a modern bottom-dwelling carpet shark.
“They would probably just wait at the bottom and then when prey comes around, they would just suck it in,” he said.

title: A Hidden Molecular Pathway Could Change How a Deadly Disease Is Treated
content:
Dissociation of the four-part TTR protein. The energy landscape shows stable states toward the bottom and unstable transition states toward the top. In the canonical pathway (red), the tetramer (T) dissociates via a native-like, compact transition state (‡1) into transient dimer intermediates (D) before full dissociation into monomers (M). In the newly discovered alternative pathway (blue), the tetramer dissociates through a more expanded transition state (‡2) directly into monomers. Credit: Jan-Hannes Schäfer, Scripps Research
Researchers have found that acidic conditions may trigger an overlooked molecular process, offering new clues about how certain disease-causing protein mutations behave.
Scientists have discovered that a protein responsible for a potentially fatal disease can unravel through a previously unknown molecular pathway. The finding, reported by researchers at Scripps Research, could help explain why certain rare inherited forms of transthyretin amyloid disease (ATTR) behave differently and raises questions about how well existing treatments address them.
ATTR develops when the protein transthyretin (TTR) loses its normal structure, misfolds, and accumulates in organs, particularly the heart and nervous system. TTR ordinarily transports vitamin A and the thyroid hormone thyroxine through the blood, cerebrospinal fluid, and eye. Its structure consists of four protein units that can separate into pairs and eventually individual units capable of forming harmful aggregates.
Scientists Discover a Second Pathway for Protein Unfolding
Until now, research had largely focused on this stepwise breakdown of TTR. The new study, published September 8, 2026, in the
Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
, demonstrates that some forms of the protein can unfold through a more direct pathway that bypasses the intermediate pairs.
To identify this alternative route, researchers examined more than 100 TTR variants, measuring their unfolding rates under different acidity levels and concentrations of urea, a chemical used to destabilize proteins. They combined these experiments with cryogenic electron microscopy and previously published X-ray crystal structures. The alternative pathway was particularly accessible in certain inherited variants associated with amyloid deposits in the brain.
Acidic Conditions and Genetic Mutations Influence the Process
The newly identified pathway becomes more favorable in acidic environments, including those inside lysosomes. These cellular compartments break down and recycle proteins, suggesting that the alternative unfolding process may serve a normal biological function.
“This route probably evolved so TTR can be degraded, which is important, but can also have side effects,” says co-author Martin Gruebele, a professor emeritus of chemistry at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign.
For the most common forms of ATTR, this pathway appears too slow under normal physiological conditions to compete with the established route. Certain disease-associated mutations, however, make it more accessible even at the acidity levels normally found in blood. Researchers have not yet established whether this alternative unfolding process directly contributes to harmful protein aggregation in patients.
What the Discovery Could Mean for ATTR Treatments
One of the most widely used ATTR treatments, tafamidis, works by stabilizing TTR’s four-unit structure, slowing its disassembly and subsequent aggregation. The discovery of another unfolding pathway raises the possibility that some rare hereditary variants may require different therapeutic approaches, although the implications for treatment effectiveness remain uncertain.
“We need to understand whether this alternative pathway can lead to TTR aggregation in the cerebrospinal fluid, which could potentially translate into worse outcomes for patients carrying these rare mutations who take the current medications,” says senior author Jeffery Kelly, the H. Lutcher Brown Endowed Chair at Scripps Research who co-developed tafamidis.
“More research is needed, but this opens up a new direction in the field of drugs targeting specific amyloidosis pathways,” says Gruebele. “At least we have one of several possible smoking guns to look at.”
Beyond ATTR, the experiments provide evidence that a protein composed of multiple subunits can follow distinct unfolding pathways in solution. Although scientists have long proposed that proteins can fold and unfold through multiple routes, experimentally demonstrating this behavior has been challenging.
“Transthyretin is the first oligomeric protein for which pathway multiplicity has been shown in solution, and without mechanical pulling,” says Marcus Jäger, the study’s first author.
Reference: “Transthyretin can denature by an alternative pathway” by Marcus Jäger, Jan-Hannes Schäfer, Gabriel C. Lander, Evan T. Powers, Martin Gruebele and Jeffery W. Kelly, 8 September 2026,
Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
DOI: 10.1073/pnas.2536532123
This work was supported by the National Institutes of Health (grant R01 DK046335) and a postdoctoral fellowship from the German Research Foundation (Project No.: 556478029).

title: The Brain Is More Capable of Healing Itself Than Scientists Thought
content:
The image on the left shows a brain lesion (diameter: just under 0.5 mm). Around the perimeter of the lesion, the newly discovered “regenerative” astrocytes begin to seal the defect by forming long cellular extensions (shown in red). Newly formed cell nuclei (shown in blue) migrate along the cellular extensions toward the damaged area. Unaltered astrocytes (shown in green) surround the lesion area. The image on the right shows an enlargement of the marked area in the left image. Credit: Institute of Pharmacology and Toxicology, University of Zurich
Researchers have uncovered a surprising cellular process that could reshape our understanding of brain regeneration and offer new possibilities for recovery from neurological damage.
Scientists have discovered an unexpected way the adult brain may replace certain cells lost to injury or disease. In living mice, researchers observed specialized brain cells repairing damaged regions by transporting newly formed cell nuclei over long distances, revealing a regenerative process that was previously unknown.
The discovery challenges the long-held belief that the adult brain cannot fully replace lost astrocytes. These star-shaped glial cells support neurons by supplying nutrients, helping regulate blood flow, and maintaining healthy brain tissue. Astrocytes can be destroyed by brain injuries and autoimmune conditions, including the rare disorder neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder, in which the body’s antibodies attack these essential cells.
Specialized Brain Cells Help Restore Damaged Tissue
A research team led by Bruno Weber at the University of Zurich (UZH) identified a specialized population of “regenerative” astrocytes in the brains of living mice. Located along the edges of damaged tissue, these cells help replace missing astrocytes and rebuild the networks that support surrounding neurons. The study’s co-lead authors were Marina Herwerth and Matthias Wyss from the university’s Institute of Pharmacology and Toxicology.
“The findings of our study reveal a previously unknown ability of the adult brain to repair itself. They point toward new ways of supporting recovery from ailments involving the loss of astrocytes,” Weber says.
An Unusual Mechanism for Brain Cell Regeneration
To investigate how this repair process works, the scientists monitored living mouse brains over several weeks using two-photon microscopy, an imaging technique that allows researchers to examine cells within living tissue. They also mapped gene activity across different brain regions to identify the astrocytes involved in regeneration.
The observations revealed that these cells do more than simply divide to produce replacements. Newly formed nuclei from daughter cells travel through the long, branching extensions of astrocytes toward areas where cells have been lost. As Weber explains, “they send the newly formed nuclei of their daughter cells gliding across long distances to repopulate the damaged area of the brain and knit the astrocyte network back together.”
New Molecular Targets Could Guide Future Treatments
“We were able to identify numerous genes and signaling pathways that are temporarily activated during repair. They could serve as starting points in the future for influencing post-disease and -injury regeneration processes,” Weber stresses.
Reference: “Focal astrocyte loss reveals nuclear translocation during lesion repopulation” by Marina Herwerth, Matthias T. Wyss, Nicola B. Schmid, Anna Lasne, Jacqueline Condrau, Luca Ravotto, José María Mateos Melero, Andres Kaech, Gustav Bredell, Carolina Thomas, Rachel Kim, Petra Kukanja, Vladyslav L. Korobeynyk, Christine Stadelmann, Thomas Misgeld, Jeffrey L. Bennett, Sebastian Jessberger, Aiman S. Saab, Shane A. Liddelow and Bruno Weber, 23 July 2026,
Nature Neuroscience
DOI: 10.1038/s41593-026-02354-5

title: Scientists Discover Never-Before-Seen Molecules With Cancer-Fighting Potential
content:
Researchers have identified a bacterial molecule that interacts with a human protein linked to cancer. Credit: Shutterstock
Scientists have uncovered a previously unknown class of natural compounds hidden within soil-dwelling bacteria.
Scientists have discovered a previously unknown group of molecules in soil bacteria that bind to a human protein associated with several types of cancer. The compounds, known as myxoglucamides, have an unusual chemical structure and could provide a starting point for developing new drugs, although researchers have not demonstrated a strong effect on cancer cell growth.
The discovery emerged from two studies examining how bacteria produce these molecules and how they interact with human cells. Myxoglucamides combine molecular components derived from sugars, lipids, and amino acids in an arrangement unlike previously known natural products. Accessing them required researchers to activate bacterial genes that normally remain silent.
Unlocking Hidden Chemistry in Soil Bacteria
Myxoglucamides are produced by myxobacteria, a group of soil-dwelling microorganisms known for synthesizing diverse biologically active compounds. Using modern genetic techniques, scientists at the Helmholtz Institute for Pharmaceutical Research Saarland (HIPS) activated a previously silent biosynthetic pathway, allowing them to produce and detect the molecules.
The team then examined the biosynthetic gene cluster responsible for their production and traced the biochemical reactions involved. Their analysis identified a previously unknown pathway in which several enzymes work together in an unexpected sequence to assemble the compounds’ distinctive chemical structure. The findings could help researchers locate other natural products concealed within inactive microbial genes.
“The discovery of myxoglucamides highlights how much chemical potential remains hidden in previously silent biosynthetic gene clusters of microorganisms,” says Dr Chengzhang Fu, head of the junior research group “Genome Mining for Secondary Metabolites” at HIPS. “By selectively activating and deciphering these biosynthetic pathways, we can gain access to entirely new natural products.”
The initial discovery and structural characterization were carried out by a team led by Prof. Rolf Müller, scientific director of HIPS and head of its Department of Microbial Natural Products.
Recreating a Rare Bacterial Molecule in the Laboratory
Because the bacteria naturally produce only tiny amounts of myxoglucamides, researchers needed another way to obtain enough material for biological testing. In the second study, they achieved the first total laboratory synthesis of myxoglucamide A, making it possible to investigate the compound and prepare chemically modified versions.
Some of these synthetic derivatives bound substantially more strongly than the original molecule to a human protein called AKR1C3. Using a method that systematically identifies which cellular proteins interact with a compound, the researchers established AKR1C3 as the primary binding target of myxoglucamides.
AKR1C3 participates in the production of certain hormones and inflammatory signaling molecules. It is also overproduced in several cancers, where it can contribute to tumor cell growth. Although binding to this protein suggests a potential direction for anticancer drug development, the experiments did not establish that myxoglucamides strongly inhibit cancer cell growth.
“Although we were unable to demonstrate a strong effect of myxoglucamides on cancer cell growth, the study nevertheless shows that natural products without an immediately obvious biological effect can still engage highly relevant targets in the human body,” says Prof Mark Brönstrup, head of the department “Chemical Biology” at HZI. “This is exactly where great potential lies for identifying new concepts for the development of innovative drugs.”

title: First Solar licenses CubicPV’s US perovskite patents
content:
First Solar licenses CubicPV’s US perovskite patents
First Solar
has signed a non-exclusive patent licensing agreement with
, giving it access to CubicPV’s issued and pending US patents on perovskite solar technology. The license applies to the sales and distribution of perovskite-based PV products in the US, covering the utility-scale, commercial and industrial, and residential markets. Other terms were not disclosed.
The agreement follows the
patent license First Solar signed with Oxford PV
in February 2026, and further clears the path for First Solar’s development of PV devices built with a perovskite semiconductor.
“Commercializing the next generation of PV takes two things. It takes the technology development and manufacturing scaling work our R&D teams are focused on, and it takes freedom to operate, which is what this agreement helps secure,” said Mark Widmar, First Solar’s CEO.
Tim McCaffery, CubicPV’s CEO, said, “Access to intellectual property is vital as the industry begins commercializing perovskite and tandem technologies. First Solar’s decision to license our IP is evidence of that shift and shows the relevance of our IP portfolio to the perovskite ecosystem.”
First Solar has a perovskite development line at its campus in Perrysburg, Ohio, which produces small-form-factor modules and which the company says has met internal milestones for initial efficiency, stability and manufacturability. It is also investing in a larger pilot line in Ohio, capable of producing modules equivalent in size to its Series 6 module, which is expected to reach operational readiness in the first half of 2027.
CubicPV, based in Bedford, Massachusetts, says it has spent more than a decade developing perovskite technology and has built a substantial portfolio of foundational patents. The company is advancing perovskite tandem technology.

and Choshu Industry are among the companies that will receive backing, which is planned to run through fiscal year 2029.

title: 国家能源局：加快推动以本地消纳为主的第二、三批大基地建设 力争2027年底基本建成投产-索比光伏网
content:
10月30日，国家能源局举行新闻发布会，介绍前三季度全国能源形势及发展成效、可再生能源并网运行、电力市场交易、迎峰度冬电力保供举措等情况，并回答记者提问。
会上，新能源和可再生能源司副司长桂小阳介绍，2021年至2023年，我局会同国家发展改革委先后印发三批以沙漠、戈壁、荒漠地区为重点的大型风电光伏基地项目清单。这三批大基地主要是以本地消纳为主，建设工作取得积极成效。截至2026年9月底，第一批大基地9453万千瓦项目，已经基本建成投产;第二批大基地建成超3400万千瓦;第三批大基地建成超2900万千瓦。三批大基地合计建成规模超1.57亿千瓦。
同时，国家发展改革委、国家能源局编制以沙漠、戈壁、荒漠地区为重点的大型风电光伏基地规划布局方案，推动千万千瓦级大基地开发建设。这类大基地以外送消纳为主，目前我们已经批复14个基地的实施方案，其中新疆天山北麓基地(疆电入渝)、宁夏腾格里沙漠基地(宁电入湘)已相继投运。西北的风光正在送往中东部的千家万户。“沙戈荒”大基地作为全国新型电力系统的重要组成部分、“西电东送”的重要实现形式，其经济社会效益正在随着项目逐步投运逐渐显现。
从当前“沙戈荒”大基地运行情况看，规模化、集约化、以新能源为主的开发模式提高了整体开发效率，降低了开发成本，在促进产业发展、推动能源清洁低碳转型和保障电力供应的同时带动了当地就业，同时推动了沙漠、戈壁、荒漠地区生态修复，在生态治理等方面发挥了重要的综合效益。
下一步，我们一方面将加快推动以本地消纳为主的第二、三批大基地建设，力争2027年底基本建成投产。另一方面，积极推进千万千瓦级“沙戈荒”大基地建设。坚持“全国一盘棋”，结合全国电力流向，统筹谋划后续“沙戈荒”新能源基地规划布局，并按照新能源、支撑性调节性电源、输电通道“三位一体”要求，协同推进基地及配套建设，为加快构建新型电力系统、实现“双碳”目标提供有力支撑。我的回答就到这里，谢谢大家!

content:
西北的电点亮长三角的灯
近日，中国电建参建的
世界首条柔性特高压直流输电工程
甘肃至浙江±800千伏特高压直流输电工程
为西北清洁能源直送长三角
“陇电入浙”工程是“十四五”电力发展规划重点工程，也是国家“西电东送”战略骨干通道，起于甘肃武威换流站，止于浙江绍兴越州换流站，途经甘肃、宁夏、陕西、河南、安徽、浙江6省（区），线路全长2370公里，额定输电容量800万千瓦，预计2027年建成投运。
作为世界首条在送受两端均采用柔性直流输电技术的跨区特高压直流输电工程，该工程可灵活调节电流大小和方向，适应大规模新能源接入电网需求。
“陇电入浙”河南段起于河南省南阳市西峡县西坪镇陕豫省界，止于河南省信阳市固始县黎集镇豫皖省界，线路长度545千米，占工程线路总长的近四分之一。沿线电力线路、高速公路、电气化铁路众多，涉及跨（钻）越110千伏以上线路80条次，500千伏及以上线路15条次，高铁、铁路、高速公路18处，需实施二级风险作业18项、三级风险作业2508项。
中国电建所属湖北工程公司承担的线路监理包6段，横跨河南省南阳市、信阳市，依次途经桐柏县等8个县级行政区，全长256.575公里，新建杆塔532基。
建设期间，项目部严格落实“事前严审、事中严控、事后严验”全链条监理模式，从严审核专项施工方案，强化作业人员资质、施工工器具、甲供物资设备核查验收；对铁塔组立、导地线展放、重大交叉跨越等高风险工序实行全程旁站。
同步践行生态环境保护主体责任，落实环水保“三同时”制度，重点盯控表土剥离、耕地复垦、渣土处置、植被恢复等关键环节，常态化开展环水保现场巡查，督促施工单位落实各项绿色施工举措，以全过程、全要素管控保障标段安全优质贯通。
工程预计将于2027年建成投运，届时甘肃每年可向浙江输送电量超360亿千瓦时，其中绿电占比超过50%，可促进新能源电量消纳超212亿千瓦时，替代燃煤消耗640万吨，减少二氧化碳排放1700万吨，充分释放甘肃清洁能源资源优势，为优化全国能源配置、助力“双碳”目标提供重要支撑。

title: Huisman secures crane contract for Siem Industries' new offshore vessels
content:
Heavy construction equipment manufacturer Huisman has been contracted by
Siem Industries to deliver knuckle boom cranes for a pair of newbuild offshore
vessels.
Under the agreement, Huisman will supply two 400mt knuckle boom cranes,
each featuring a below-deck winch, along with two 50mt auxiliary cranes.
All of the cranes will be built at the company's production facility in
Zhangzhou, China.
The 400mt cranes feature full-load active heave compensation, deepwater
capabilities, a high-lift mode, LiDAR based active collision avoidance
and reduced power demand on the vessel's electrical grid.
According to the announcement these features are designed to enhance efficiency
and reliability in offshore lifting operations while providing the versatility
required for a wide range of offshore activities.
David Roodenburg, CEO of Huisman, said: “We greatly appreciate the continued
confidence Siem places in our company and are honoured to continue our
partnership through the award of this contract.
“We look forward to delivering cranes that will support Siem Shipping's
operations and future ambitions.”

title: South Korea launches 2.2GW offshore wind auction round
content:
South Korea’s Ministry of Climate, Energy and Environment has opened competitive
bidding for fixed-price offshore wind contracts covering approximately
2.2GW of capacity in the second half of 2026.
The auction includes around 1.7GW of fixed-bottom offshore wind capacity,
comprising 1.4GW under a general track and 300MW under a public-led track.
A separate floating offshore wind track will offer approximately 500MW
of capacity.
The latest round follows a 1.8GW auction held in the first half of this
year, bringing the total offshore wind tender volume for 2026 to 4GW.
The government said the increased auction volumes are intended to improve
market predictability, support economies of scale and strengthen investment
confidence.
For public-led projects, public institutions must hold a minimum ownership
stake. The framework is designed to support project delivery, increase
public acceptance and promote the use of domestic supply chains for key
equipment.
The price ceiling for fixed-bottom offshore wind has been set at 168.937
won/kWh, while floating offshore wind projects will face a ceiling of 174.003
won/kWh. Both limits are lower than those applied in the first half of
The government is also reviewing an extension of offshore wind fixed-price
contract terms from 20 years to 25 years in future auction rounds.

title: Two floating offshore wind projects receive NOK 3.9 Billion in Enova funding
content:
Two floating offshore wind projects receive NOK 3.9 Billion in Enova funding TGS 4C | 4C Offshore News
Two floating offshore wind projects receive NOK 3.9 Billion in Enova funding
Two floating offshore wind projects have received a combined NOK 3.9 billion
in funding from Enova to support installation activities over the next
five years.
Fortius Offshore Wind AS and Fram Wind Solutions AS have been officially
selected to install large offshore wind turbines at the METCentre floating
offshore wind demonstration site off Karmøy, according to an October 30
announcement.
The four turbines are expected to generate enough electricity to match
the annual consumption of around 15,000 households. Each turbine will have
an installed capacity of 18.5 MW.
Enova has allocated NOK 2 billion to Fortius Offshore Wind AS and NOK 1.94
billion to Fram Wind Solutions AS. The projects were selected through a
competitive process based on the amount of energy generated per krone of
funding.
Earlier this year, Enova announced that five companies had applied for
the funding, highlighting continued industry interest in floating offshore
wind despite ongoing challenges in the sector.
According to Enova, the projects will test new technologies, including
floating foundations for large turbines and new construction and installation
methods, with the aim of improving the long-term profitability of floating
offshore wind.
"If they succeed in making offshore wind technology profitable enough,
it will be a major step toward faster, large-scale deployment of renewable
power," said Evy Glørstad, CEO of Enova.

title: An Anthropic Windfall Could Await State Pension Funds
content: Over the past year, politicians and AI executives have floated ideas for a sovereign wealth fund or other ways of giving the American public a stake in the AI boom. Some of the biggest public pension plans are poised to get a taste of the action long before those proposals come to fruition. Pension plans representing public employees in Orange County, Los Angeles, Massachusetts and South Carolina are positioned to get sizeable payouts from Anthropic’s expected initial public offering in November, thanks to the investments they made in one big Anthropic backer, Spark Capital, according to an analysis from The Information. The cash returns would represent a bright spot for what’s been a fairly bleak period for payouts to the pensions and endowments that invest in venture funds, known as limited partners. One common measure of those payouts is distributions to paid-in capital, a ratio of how much cash a venture fund has returned to its limited partners relative to what they invested in their funds. The average DPI for venture funds raised in 2021 was a mere 0.05 times at the end of last year—the lowest five-year DPI multiple this century, according to data firm PitchBook. Cash payouts have fallen because tech IPOs have been few and far between over the past few years, and high valuations on startups during the low-interest-rate era between 2020 and 2021 made it harder to sell some companies. But SpaceX’s blockbuster June IPO, which valued the rocket company at $1.75 trillion, and Anthropic’s imminent listing at an expected $1.5 trillion valuation, stand to improve those cash distributions. Harvard University’s endowment in August, for instance, disclosed a $2.2 billion stake in SpaceX. In the case of SpaceX, payouts to limited partners could result from endowments that invested directly in the startups or through funds run by SpaceX venture capital investors DFJ Growth, Valor Equity Partners, Founders Fund and Sequoia Capital , which stood to reap tens of billions of dollars. The same is true for Anthropic. Spark Capital’s Winning Funds Spark Capital first invested in Anthropic’s Series C in early 2023, an effort led by General Partner Yasmin Razavi. Over six financings, the firm plunged around $777 million into the model maker via at least three funds. Spark could haul in $9 billion or more from the investments. Pension funds that invested in Spark’s earlier funds stand to gain the most. Orange County Employees Retirement System committed $33.3 million into the Spark Capital Growth Fund IV, a 2021 fund with a $1.3 billion target, according to public filings; the Los Angeles City Employees’ Retirement System also committed $33.3 million to that Spark fund, which invested in Anthropic’s 2023 fundraise as well as the 2024 one, when the company was valued around $20 billion. The Los Angeles City Employees’ Retirement System and the Orange County Employees Retirement System invested around $33 million each into Spark Capital Growth Fund V. That fund, raised in 2023 with a $1.4 billion target, backed three Anthropic rounds in 2025 and 2026, according to the public disclosures. As Spark kept investing in the fast-growing Anthropic, the venture firm’s limited partners kept investing as well. A fund representing pension assets of Massachusetts teachers and other public employees voted to commit up to $42 million to Spark Capital Growth VI, raised in 2026 with a $1.95 billion target. South Carolina Retirement System also backed the Spark fund, which invested in Anthropic’s fundraise early this year, valuing it at $965 billion. Spark put almost $440 million in that round. Of course, cash payouts will likely take a while, given the complicated series of restrictions on selling shares that last up to a year after the IPO. The size of each pension funds’ Anthropic stake couldn’t be learned. Still, that doesn’t seem to have diminished the desire of public pension funds to come back for more. The Massachusetts Pension Reserves Investment Management approved and the South Carolina Retirement System recently committed $18 million and $30 million, respectively, to back Spark Capital IX, a new fund the firm is raising. The Information reported in March that Spark is raising a new $3 billion fund.

title: Behind DeepSeek’s $16 Billion Funding: Chinese Tech Titans and State Players
content: Chinese AI star DeepSeek’s nearly $16 billion funding round this month involved not only a deluge of capital but a who’s who of Chinese tech investors—and some of the country’s most powerful state-backed institutions, according to details of the round obtained by The Information. It was only the second fundraising round for DeepSeek. The three-year-old company was the only major AI model developer to eschew external capital until its first fundraising in April. The new round included previous backers—Tencent and battery maker CATL continue to be DeepSeek’s top two investors—but also other tech companies including notably memory chipmaker ChangXin Memory Technologies and its chairman Zhu Yiming, according to the details provided by two people with direct knowledge of the matter. Notably, Chinese state-owned investors accounted for 27% of the 105.5 billion yuan ($15.8 billion) from nearly 30 investors in this new round, which valued DeepSeek at 615.5 billion yuan. While DeepSeek is a privately owned company started by entrepreneur Liang Wenfeng, that figure—up from 2% in DeepSeek’s first fundraising—could reinforce suspicions in the U.S. that DeepSeek’s competition with leading American AI companies is driven in part by the Chinese government’s agenda. DeepSeek doubled the size of the latest round in the middle of fundraising, due mainly to the surging prices of Nvidia ’s Blackwell chips on the black market, according to the two people. The cost of a server containing eight B300 chips climbed to about 19 million yuan ($2.85 million) from 15 million yuan in the four months DeepSeek was raising the round—more than five times what the same machine sells in most countries, according to chip smugglers. Another reason for DeepSeek to increase the round size was to build a warchest for a rainy day in case the AI bubble bursts, the two people said. Already, MiniMax and Zhipu, known as Z.ai , the first two Chinese model developers to go public, have seen their market values plunge since the summer, when restrictions on sales from pre-IPO investors expired. DeepSeek has now raised 136.5 billion yuan in about six months, and Liang pumped another 2 billion yuan into the company. Although that total is dwarfed by what Anthropic and OpenAI have raised, it remains the largest venture capital fundraising by a Chinese AI firm to date. The blitzing funding pace became possible thanks largely to backing from Chinese tech incumbents spanning internet, electric vehicle, chipmaking and social media. A slew of Chinese tech companies joined the latest round. In addition to ChangXin, state-backed foundry Semiconductor Manufacturing International Corp participated, marking alliances with two powerful Chinese chip giants that make sense at a time when DeepSeek and other Chinese model developers are battling a compute shortage caused by U.S. export controls on advanced AI chips and a global deficit of memory chips. Other, less obvious tech backers included smartphone maker Vivo, food delivery giant Meituan, home appliances retailer Midea, iPhone supplier Luxshare, carmaker Geely, travel website Ctrip and social media network Xiaohongshu, also known as RedNote. These companies contributed between 1 billion and 3 billion yuan each. In total, tech companies have footed 42% of DeepSeek’s two funding rounds combined. State-backed investors have accounted for 19%. China’s National Artificial Intelligence Development Fund wrote another 1 billion yuan check in the second round, same as the first fundraising. The fund invested directly in DeepSeek, a contrast with most other investors. In DeepSeek’s first fundraising, it employed an unusual deal structure where all investors except for the National AI fund had to put their money in an entity owned by Liang, forfeiting their voting rights and committing to locking up their shares for five years unless the company goes public before then, The Information reported previously . But the National AI fund is by no means DeepSeek’s biggest state-backed financier to date. State-owned telecom carriers China Mobile and China Telecom, as well as China International Capital Corp. and Citic Securites—two of the country’s top investment banks—and insurer China Life wrote checks ranging from 2 billion to 8 billion yuan. China’s venture capital and private equity firms together only come in third in their combined stakes in DeepSeek. The biggest checks were written by Beijing-based Monolith Management, led by former Sequoia Capital China partner Cao Xi. IDG Capital invested in a total of 6.5 billion in the two rounds. Boyu Capital, co-founded by Alvin Jiang, grandson of late Chinese leader Jiang Zemin, participated in the second round with 3.5 billion yuan.
